In contrast, the CPPR resin system developed in this work rebounds spontaneously at
room temperature without any external field after an ultrahigh compressive strain of
75%, restoring both its shape and load-bearing function (strength) within 4–5 min.
This “high-load, room-temperature self-recovery” condition is not directly comparable to
FDM systems, which are mostly triggered above their T . Accordingly, the manuscript
g
emphasises the fundamental differences in load level and environmental boundary
conditions, highlighting the engineering significance of our stress-release-driven self-
recovery without external heating.
(2) Comparison of the “mechanical ceiling” with DIW green-crosslinked
nanocellulose structural components (SI Table 5): DIW, high-solids-content
nanocellulose parts employing citric acid (CA) green crosslinking followed by
esterification can reach a flexural strength and modulus of 82.78 MPa and 6.97 GPa
(ADMI 2022), respectively, while more recent DIW lignin/nanocellulose composites
achieve 102.93 MPa/9.05 GPa (ACS Omega 2024). These studies are primarily
positioned as structural materials (high strength and shape fidelity) and do not
systematically report SME metrics. In contrast, the proposed CPPR resin system
achieves a compressive strength of 115.42 MPa within a photocured network while
simultaneously combining high strength, toughness, and recoverability. By using DLP
printing, we obtain a single resin system that provides both high mechanical strength
and complex shape-memory responses, representing an advancement in coupled
performance rather than a mere competition in strength or stiffness.
(3) Comparison of manufacturability/resolution with other sustainable
photoresins: The thiolactone-based circular photoresin reported in Nature (2024)
demonstrates high-fidelity printing with 30 µm pixels, 50 µm layer thickness, and 100
µm wall thickness, demonstrating that high resolution and cross-platform
manufacturability can be achieved via sustainable chemistry routes. In this work, our
customised DLP setup achieves a minimum feature size on the order of ~5 µm,
together with efficient fabrication at a conventional 50 µm/layer and 8 s/layer. Thus,
in terms of resolution, our system is on the same order, or even finer in terms of minimum feature
size, than these state-of-the-art formulations reported in top-tier journals.
(4) Recovery mode and temperature window: The distinctive feature of the proposed
CPPR resin system is the coexistence of: (i) rapid stress-release-driven rebound at room
temperature, (ii) high load-bearing capacity and stiffness (compressive strength ≈
115.42 MPa; E_tensile ≈1.40 GPa), (iii) reproducible printing resolution and process
parameters (50 μm, 8 s per layer), and (iv) stability in aqueous environments. This
profile is complementary to most academically reported thermally triggered SMPs or
low-modulus soft networks, e.g., cardanol-based networks, E ≈ 0.2–2 MPa. Our
CPPR-P maintains a relatively high storage modulus (DMA) in the room-to-medium
temperature range (0–100°C), with a Tg of ~90°C, indicating better suitability for
structural applications at elevated service temperatures. The results indicate that, under
a “heavy-load, thick-section” condition of 75% compressive strain, the samples can
fully recover their overall shape within 4–5 min, which is an appropriate recovery
timescale for thick, load-bearing components.
The olive-oil-based system reported in AFM 2025 exhibits a Tg of around 20–25°C
(higher Tg₂) and achieves recovery within 40–100 s. It offers advantages in rapid
response for thinner parts in a mild temperature window, rendering it suitable for
constrained conditions such as biomedical use. The work published in Nat. Commun.
2023 provides a cold-programming strategy with multi-stage activatable transitions (Tc
= 62/42/<0°C), highlighting cutting-edge capabilities in programming freedom and
manufacturability of complex architectures. In this context, the proposed CPPR resin
system differs from previous studies in both the application domain and response
regime and is complementary to them.
(5) Mechanical benchmarks: In this work, a compressive strength and modulus of
115.42 MPa and 1.404 GPa, respectively, represent a rare combination of high load-
bearing capacity and recoverability among bio-based SMPs. For instance, in other
studies: the lipoate system reported in Nat. 2024 follows a circular reprinting route and
demonstrates a thermal/mechanical window comparable to commercial products, but
does not primarily target SMP metrics; the work published in Sci. Adv. 2024 presents
extreme stretchability (>1400%), but is not bio-based.
(6) Printing resolution/complexity (precision): In this work, we have achieved a
process resolution of 5 μm under DLP conditions, facilitated an integrated
demonstration of design–fabrication–performance. This resolution contrasts favourably
with the highest precision reported in comparative studies (e.g., Nat. 2024), which
involved a systematic evaluation of dimensional deviation and z-direction cure depth
at a pixel size of 30 μm. This capability highlights that our system is exceptionally well-
suited for highly customised, high-precision structural printing. It further suggests that
the established pixel/layer-thickness–to–dimensional-accuracy data from those prior
works can be leveraged for benchmarking our own high-resolution prints.
FDM relies predominantly on thermal or magnetic triggering for rapid (second-scale)
recovery, but its printing resolution and ability to form complex topologies are
inherently constrained by nozzle geometry and the layer-by-layer deposition path. DIW
systems, while excelling in strength and shape fidelity due to green-crosslinked
nanocellulose, rarely report key shape-memory effect (SME) metrics. DLP/SLA offer
advantages in resolution, complex microstructures, and scalability. Our work
demonstrates that, even when biomass is utilised as the primary feedstock, it is still
possible to achieve strength–shape-memory coupled performance on the same order as
established engineering thermosets.
From the perspective of matching materials, structures, and service conditions, CPPR
is biased toward higher service temperatures, high load-bearing capacity, and thick-
walled components, in contrast with other bio-based systems that have their own
optimal temperature windows and application scenarios and target in vivo/mild-
temperature environments with rapid response. In terms of sustainability, this study
aligns with the closed-loop remanufacturing concept reported in Nature 2024,
highlighting the potential for cyclic utilisation of cellulose segments and developing
recycle–reprint strategies (e.g., swelling/recovery and possible re-use of chain segments)
as a promising avenue for future sustainable development.

5. The authors attribute the tensile-strength increase after 100 days in water to

Our response: We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to clarify the mechanism
underlying the tensile strength increase after long-term water immersion and
subsequent drying. We performed a comprehensive post-immersion analysis on printed
CPPR-P parts after 100 days in water and added the results to the SI. Jointly, the data
support a dual-mechanism: limited hydrolytic scission at accessible ester/urethane sites
plus removal of low-Mw sol fraction, followed by dry-state reinforcement via denser
H-bonding/rearrangement. This combination rationalises the observed increase in
tensile strength after drying.
Added evidences:
(1) FTIR (bulk surface, ATR): After 100 days of immersion in water and subsequent
drying, the FTIR spectra demonstrated (i) a broadened O–H band (~3200–3600
cm⁻¹) and (ii) a growth/shift of C=O features (~1700–1730 cm⁻¹) with a shoulder
consistent with –COOH/–O–C=O. However, C–O–C intensity (~1150 cm⁻¹) decreased,
consistent with mild hydrolysis and formation of more H-bond donors/acceptors in the
Fig.R6 (SI Fig. S21).

component (~288.5 eV in C1s; ~532.5 eV in O1s), indicating again the formation

was controlled by identical cleaning/charge-ref settings in the Fig.R7 (SI Fig. S16).

Fig.R8 (SI Fig. S17).

The CPPR-P absorbs water but retains its integrity, reaching a plateau swelling of ≈
26–29%. This is indicative of a densely crosslinked acrylate–cellulose network with
limited free volume. The modest ≈17% mass loss after 48 h reflects the extraction of
residual oligomers/sol fractions plus minor hydrolysis of surface ester linkages.
Moreover, the absence of disintegration corroborates the robust covalent crosslink
density. Together with our mechanical data, these results confirm that CPPR-P is a
water-stable, high-strength photoresin suitable for printed parts operating in humid or
aqueous environments. Furthermore, they confirm that the CPPR crosslinked network
is water-stable (no disintegration) while allowing controlled water uptake, consistent
with its covalent network plus reversible H-bonding. The test details have been inserted
in the Methods section and referenced the new SI tables in the Results.
Water exposure induces localised hydrolysis at more accessible ester linkages
(primarily at chain ends/defects), generating –OH/–COOH groups that increase H-
bond density and facilitate chain packing upon drying. In parallel, leaching of low-
M_w plasticising species (and minor post-curing) raises Tg and E′, yielding a
stiffer, stronger network. Thus, the strength increase is not due to wholesale
backbone degradation, but to hydrolysis-assisted purification and H-bond
reorganisation within a stable crosslinked matrix.
Taken together, these pieces of evidence point to mild hydrolysis plus soluble
oligomer migration, followed by the formation of stronger hydrogen bonding and
chain rearrangement upon drying, which rationalises the observed increase in
tensile strength.
The corresponding data and discussion have been incorporated into the main
manuscript and SI.

1. In the synthetic protocols, workup details are still missing. How were the final
products isolated and recovered from the reaction? How did the authors made sure
that the product was pure?
Our response: We appreciate the reviewer’s request and agree that the previous version
did not describe the workup/purification steps with sufficient operational detail. In the
revised manuscript and SI, we now explicitly clarify how each intermediate/product
was isolated and how residual small molecules were removed and verified.
Step 1 (epichlorohydrin grafting / MCC-E): removal of unreacted ECH. After
completion of the epichlorohydrin ring-opening grafting, the key workup objective is
to eliminate residual epichlorohydrin, which is volatile. The reaction mixture is cooled
to room temperature and the remaining epichlorohydrin is removed by rotary
evaporation (Vacuum degree 220-250Pa, 75 ℃, rotation speed 20, time 45 minutes)
under reduced pressure until a constant mass (or no further condensate) is observed.
This step effectively prevents carryover of unreacted ECH into Step 2 and ensures safe
handling and reproducibility.
Step 2 (HEMA grafting / CPPR precursor): removal of unreacted HEMA and acid
catalyst. After the HEMA grafting reaction, the workup aims to remove (i) unreacted
HEMA and (ii) the acid catalyst. We accomplish this by a combination of reduced-
pressure rotary evaporation (Vacuum degree 500-600Pa, 60 ℃, rotation speed 20, time
60-90 minutes) (to remove residual HEMA) and neutralization (Add triethylamine
dropwise at room temperature (1.05 equivalents relative to the acid), and stir for 10-15
minutes, to quench the acid catalyst. And the mixture was passed through a short plug
of basic alumina to capture the residual acid/salts.), followed by brief vacuum
treatment to remove trace volatiles. We have now explicitly described these operations
(cooling → stripping of HEMA → catalyst quench/neutralization) in the revised Step-
2 protocol.
Step 3 (resin formulation and printed-part “purification”): removal of
extractables and ensuring full cure. Step 3 produces a photocurable resin by
formulation; therefore, “product purification” relevant to materials testing is performed
on the printed parts. As described in the Methods, the as-printed objects are washed in
anhydrous ethanol to remove unreacted/soluble residues at the surface, followed by 405
nm post-curing to drive conversion to completion before characterization.
How we ensured “purity” of the precursors/products. We define purity here as the
effective removal of residual low-molecular-weight species (ECH/HEMA/catalyst)
prior to formulation and printing. Completion of small-molecule removal is confirmed
by (i) constant mass/no further distillate under vacuum, and (ii) the absence (or
negligible intensity) of characteristic vinyl signals from free HEMA in the ¹H NMR of
the soluble fraction, together with consistent spectroscopic and thermal features of the
final materials.
We do not claim absolute chemical purity for a crosslinked network; instead, we ensure
that residual small molecules are removed and extractables are minimized, and we
verify this using characterization: (i) spectroscopy confirms the expected
functionalization of the precursor and consumption of vinyl groups after curing; (ii) the
printed network becomes insoluble, and only a small soluble fraction is extractable for
GPC analysis, consistent with minimal residual low-molecular-weight species; and (iii)
thermal analysis is consistent with a stable cured network. These points are clarified
and cross-referenced in the revised manuscript and SI.
Revisions implemented: We have added a dedicated “Workup” description in the Step-
1 and Step-2 protocols to specify removal of residual epichlorohydrin, and removal of
residual HEMA plus acid catalyst, and we have cross-referenced the post-print
washing/post-curing procedure used (Step-3) to minimize extractables prior to all
characterization. These revisions are described in detail in the Methods section of the
manuscript (lines 442–494).
2. On the “Step 3” the authors wrote that “ethylene glycol dimethacrylate (EGDMA)
as a reactive co-monomer (…) and 40 wt% acrylamide (C₃H₅NO) was introduced as a
crosslinker.” Please confirm this statement. Why bisacrylamide was added?
Please provide this information in the manuscript.
Our response: Thank you for pointing out this ambiguity. We confirm that the wording
in the previous version was inaccurate and confusing. We has been corrected in the
revised manuscript. And has been corrected to use standard polymer-chemistry
terminology.
Role clarification (EGDMA vs. acrylamide): EGDMA does not refer to
“bisacrylamide”; rather, it stands for “ethylene glycol dimethacrylate”. In the original
manuscript, the imprecise wording could have led to confusion and misunderstanding
among readers. In industrial applications, EGDMA is clearly classified as a small-
molecule crosslinker used to improve the mechanical properties and thermal stability
of polymeric materials. For example, it participates in crosslinking via free-radical
reactions but does not itself form long-chain structures; rather, it functions as a small-
molecule crosslinker and a reactive additive.
In contrast, acrylamide (C₃H₅NO) is a monofunctional vinyl comonomer and reactive
diluent. Acrylamide is added primarily to (i) tune viscosity and DLP processability,
and (ii) introduce polar amide groups that strengthen intermolecular interactions (e.g.,
hydrogen bonding) and modulate thermal–mechanical behavior. We have revised Step
3 accordingly to avoid misinterpretation.
About “bisacrylamide”: No bisacrylamide was used in this work. The term
“bisacrylamide” appeared due to an unintended wording/naming confusion and has
been removed from the manuscript and SI. The only difunctional additive used
throughout the formulations is EGDMA, as also summarized in Table R1 (manuscript
Table 1) and Table S4 (SI).
Manuscript revision for clarity and reproducibility: We revised the Step 3
description and the formulation table 1 to clearly define component roles as: EGDMA:
difunctional, low-molecular-weight additive.

the manuscript, specifying “ethylene glycol dimethacrylate (EGDMA)” (Methods, Step

3. The concerns raised about the confirmation of the functionalization of MCC still
persist. How did the 13C NMR add new information? Is it possible to exclude the
presence of unreacted HEMA by the NMR results?
Our response: We appreciate this continued concern and agree that FTIR/¹H NMR
alone may not be sufficiently diagnostic for cellulose derivatives due to peak overlap
and broadening. We therefore added ¹³C NMR specifically because it provides more
structure-specific carbon environments and allows us to distinguish covalently grafted
ester/methacrylate carbons from the native cellulose backbone.
(1) What new information ¹³C NMR provides (beyond FTIR/¹H NMR).
In the revised SI, ¹³C NMR of MCC and CPPR shows: (i) the characteristic
cellulose backbone signals (C1–C6) remain, confirming the cellulose scaffold
is retained; and importantly; (ii) new resonances assigned to the ester carbonyl
carbon (–O–C(=O)–) and the methacrylate/vinyl carbons appear in CPPR,
which are absent in pristine MCC. These features directly indicate the
introduction of methacrylate ester functionality onto the cellulose-derived
precursor and therefore provide direct evidence of functionalization at the
carbon level, rather than relying only on IR band shifts or proton signals that
may overlap.
(2) Can NMR exclude unreacted HEMA? —what we can and cannot claim.
We agree that, in principle, solution-state NMR alone cannot “prove absolute
absence” of trace free HEMA in any polymer sample. However, the ¹H NMR
of the soluble fraction provides a strong practical check: free HEMA exhibits
sharp, characteristic vinyl proton peaks (typically around ~5.6–6.2 ppm) and a
distinct –CH₂–CH₂–OH pattern. In our spectra, these sharp monomer peaks are
not observed (or are negligible compared to the broad grafted signals),
indicating that free HEMA, if present, is below the NMR detection limit. To
avoid overstatement, we revised our wording (SI, Fig. S28) to: “no detectable
free HEMA in ¹H NMR of the soluble fraction after workup”.
(3) A description and discussion regarding the exclusion of unreacted
HEMA.
This NMR conclusion is consistent with our revised workup: after Step 2
(manuscript, 467-475 line), residual HEMA is removed by rotary evaporation
under reduced pressure, and the acid catalyst is quenched and removed using
a basic alumina plug before resin formulation. In addition, the cured CPPR
network becomes insoluble and only a limited extractable fraction can be
analyzed by GPC, which further supports that low-molecular-weight residues
are minimized prior to printing and testing. Therefore, the combined evidence
(workup + ¹³C NMR functionalization + ¹H NMR check for free monomer +
extractables behavior) addresses the reviewer’s concern.

7. Please provide information about how the .stl file was obtained.
Our response: We appreciate this request and have clarified the digital workflow used
to generate the printable .stl files. In our work, the initial geometry was created and
edited as a .max model (3ds Max). However, .max is not a printer-readable format and
cannot be processed directly by the DLP printing pipeline. Therefore, the model must
be exported to .stl, which is the standard triangulated mesh format accepted by slicing
and printing software.
Specifically, the workflow is:
1. Modeling (source file): the 3D geometry was constructed in Autodesk 3ds Max
and saved as .max.
2. Export to STL: the model was exported from 3ds Max as .stl (triangulated
mesh). During export, we ensured the model with consistent surface normals
and appropriate units (mm) to match the intended specimen dimensions.
3. Slicing-printing preparation: the exported .stl was then imported into the DLP
printer software, where printing parameters (layer thickness, exposure time,
base layers, etc.) were set (reported in Table S4). The software then performed
slicing to generate the layer-by-layer build file used by the printer.
To ensure reproducibility, we added this description to the SI (section of Model1) and
provided representative STL files for the standard specimens (e.g., the lattice 3D model
specimen STL file in the SI).
8. What is the explanation of the authors for the results observed in the swelling tests?
Our response: We thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion, which
significantly helps improve the scientific rigor of our manuscript. Providing an
explanation for the swelling results—particularly the increase in tensile strength after
100 days of water immersion—enables us to more clearly understand and elucidate the
hydrolytic stability and performance of the resulting materials. Order to explain the
swelling-test results and to clarify the mechanism underlying the tensile strength
increase after long-term water immersion and subsequent drying. We performed a
comprehensive post-immersion analysis on printed CPPR-P parts after 100 days in
water (manuscript, 216-221 line) and added the results to the SI. Jointly, the data

plus removal of low-Mw sol fraction, followed by dry-state reinforcement via denser

primary thermally activated transition (glass transition–type switching event)
used for the shape-memory behavior, which is consistent with the thermo-
mechanical switching observed by DMA. (iii) Curing or structure dependence:
CPPR-P (printed + post-cured) exhibits a more “network-dominated” thermal
response than CPPR-L. In particular, the printed network typically shows
reduced low-temperature relaxation features and a shift of the switching
transition toward higher temperature and/or a more pronounced ΔCp step,
consistent with higher double-bond conversion and a higher effective crosslink
density after printing/post-curing. Conversely, CPPR-L can contain small
contributions from residual monomer/low-molecular components and physical
relaxation, which are minimized after curing.

3. In the revision, the DSC curves reported in Fig. 5f correspond to the
second heating scan (after the first heating/cooling cycle) to eliminate thermal
history and to avoid misinterpretation from physical aging/enthalpy relaxation
and possible residual volatile release. This is now clearly indicated in the figure
caption and in the Methods section.
The previously shown DSC curves were replaced by newly collected data with baseline
correction and explicit reporting of the scan number. The baseline-corrected second-
run DSC reveals the dominant thermal switching transition used for the shape-memory
effect. Compared to CPPR-L, CPPR-P shows a network-reinforced thermal response,
consistent with higher conversion and higher effective crosslink density after
printing/post-curing, which suppresses relaxation contributions from low-molecular
components and enhances the switching signal.
10. Why deuterated DMSO was used as mobile phase for GPC? Not sure if GPC
information is valuable to the present manuscript.
Our response: Thank you for raising this point. First, we clarify that our GPC does not
attempt to measure the molecular weight of the entire printed CPPR network, which is
insoluble after DLP curing. Instead, GPC was performed only on the DMSO-d6-
soluble/extractable (“sol”) fraction obtained from the printed specimens, as now
explicitly stated in the SI caption (SI Fig. S30). This soluble fraction contains
unreacted/partially reacted pendant chains, oligomers, and other extractables that can
be dissolved and therefore chromatographically analyzed, whereas the load-bearing
crosslinked network remains insoluble. In this context, GPC is used as a
supportive/qualitative indicator of curing and aging behavior rather than an absolute
descriptor of the crosslinked network.
Regarding the use of DMSO-d₆, we agree that deuteration is not intrinsically required
for GPC. We used DMSO-d₆ primarily because (i) the cellulose-derived CPPR
extractables are highly polar and hydrogen-bonding, and DMSO-d6 is the most reliable
solvent to ensure complete dissolution and avoid aggregation/partial solubility artifacts
(which was the main source of uncertainty in our previous GPC traces); and (ii) DMSO-
d₆ was the high-purity DMSO available in our laboratory and was also used for the
complementary solution-state NMR characterization, allowing consistent sample
handling. Importantly, the isotopic substitution (DMSO vs. DMSO-d₆) does not change
the interpretation of our GPC results because SEC separation is governed by
hydrodynamic volume; therefore, we have revised the text to emphasize “DMSO-d6-
soluble fraction” and positioned the GPC data as supporting evidence alongside
FTIR/XPS/NMR and thermal analyses.
To address the reviewer’s concern about GPC information is valuable to the
present manuscript, we also revised the manuscript and SI wording so that GPC is not
presented as a stand-alone proof. Rather, it supports the following limited claims: (1)
after DLP curing, the extractable fraction shows an apparent shift consistent with chain
growth/network formation; and (2) after water aging, the extractable fraction shifts
toward lower molar mass with broader dispersity, consistent with mild scission in
soluble/dangling segments, while the bulk network remains intact—fully consistent
with our spectroscopic and thermal signatures (SI Fig. S30 and related discussion).

2. The synthesis of ECHMCC, UC-CPPR, and CPPR: The authors did not explain
clearly how to synthesize them step by step in Methods and Supporting Information.
MCC is crystalline cellulose, and ECHMCC seems an amorphous cellulose, as
shown in SI Figure 13. It seems that the authors dissolved MCC and performed
epoxidation. Once it is true, then the cellulose solvent could influence all of
products. The authors need to explain it.
Our response: Thank you very much for your suggestion. Upon review, we realised
that key methodological details were indeed missing, preventing a clear and
unambiguous description of the synthetic route for obtaining the photocurable resin.
We have now provided sufficient detail to ensure reproducibility of the reaction and
have incorporated this information into the Methods section of the revised manuscript
(lines 439–477). We are grateful to you for pointing out this critical omission.
Synthesis – Step 1 the prepared process of MCC epichlorohydrin.
The reaction shown in Fig. R1(Fig. S13 of the SI) corresponds to Step 1 of the synthesis.
First, an epoxide ring-opening reaction occurs between the cellulose chains and
epichlorohydrin. Briefly, 2 g of pretreated microcrystalline cellulose (MCC) was
initially allowed to swell and uniformly dispersed in 70 mL of DMSO and maintained
at 50°C in a water bath until a homogeneous suspension was obtained. Subsequently,
epichlorohydrin (40 mL) was placed in a dropping funnel and added dropwise at a rate
of 10 mL h⁻¹. Then, 15 mL of 30 wt% aqueous NaOH solution was added dropwise
over 30–45 min using a dropping funnel. The mixture was then heated to 80–85°C and
allowed to react for a further 4 h. After cooling the reaction system to room temperature,
the functionalised MCC precursor was obtained. Under alkaline conditions at 80°C, the
epoxide group of epichlorohydrin underwent a ring-opening reaction to generate
reactive sites, at which point the primary hydroxyl group at the C6 position of cellulose
reacted with it. The resulting product is named as MCC-E.
Fig. R1 Epoxide ring-opening reaction between cellulose molecules and epichlorohydrin.
Synthesis – Step 2 the synthetic of Cellulose-based photopolymerisable resin
(CPPR) precursor .
The reaction depicted in Fig. R2(Fig. 14 of the SI) corresponds to Step 2 of the
synthesis. Based on the precursor obtained in Step 1, free-radical photoreactive groups
were grafted onto the cellulose backbone. The product from Step 1 was transferred into
a 500 mL round-bottom flask and 0.5 wt% methanesulfonic acid (CH₃SO₃H) was used
as a catalyst. Subsequently, 50 wt% hydroxyethyl methacrylate(HEMA) (C₆H₁₀O₃) was
added to introduce the free-radical photoreactive grafting groups, and the mixture was
stirred at 70°C in a water bath for 6 h. After reaction completion, the system was cooled
to 50°C and maintained for a further 4 h to ensure complete conversion. The resulting
product is Cellulose-based photopolymerisable resin (CPPR) precursor used for DLP
additive manufacturing.
Fig. R2 Graft-free radical photosensitive reactive groups.
Synthesis – Step 3 the synthetic of Cellulose-based photocurable print resin liquid
(CPPR-L).
The reaction exhibited in Fig. R3(Fig. 15 of the SI) corresponds to Step 3, which details
the photo-initiated free-radical polymerisation of the CPPR resin. First, 150 mL of the
CPPR resin monomer prepared in Step 2 was transferred into a 500 mL round-bottom
flask, followed by the addition of 15 mL of ethylene glycol dimethacrylate
(EGDMA) as a reactive co-monomer for the subsequent free-radical polymerisation.
The mixture was stirred at 50°C until complete dissolution. Next, the temperature
was lowered to 30°C (to prevent premature partial polymerisation), and 40 wt%
acrylamide (C₃H₅NO) was introduced as a crosslinker. The reaction was allowed to
proceed under stirring for 30 min at 30 °C. Subsequently, 0.1 wt% N,N′-
methylenebisacrylamide (MBA) was introduced, and stirring continued for another 30 min.
Finally, 0.5 wt% TPO was added as the photoinitiator, and stirring was continued until a
homogeneous Cellulose-based photocurable print resin liquid (CPPR-L) capable of
undergoing UV-induced free-radical polymerization was obtained. The CPPR-L2 and
CPPR-L3 were fabricated according to the different content of CPPR and acrylamide.
HEMA-PR refers photocurable print resin only with HEMA. NE-CPPR refers CPPR
without MCC epichlorohydrin step.
Fig.R3 DLP-based UV curing via free radical polymerisation and crosslinking.
Regarding the issue you raised in your revision comments concerning MCC dissolution
and the change in crystallinity (SI Fig. S23), we would like to thank you for pointing
this out, as it helps make our manuscript more scientifically rigorous and easier to
follow.
First, we did not dissolve MCC in a cellulose-dissolving medium (such as DMAc/LiCl,
ionic liquids, or NaOH/urea). Step 1 is explicitly conducted in a heterogeneous
alkaline system at 80 °C, where MCC is in a swollen/dispersed state. ECH reacts with
the C6–OH groups of MCC via epoxide ring-opening etherification and results in a
small degree of interchain bridging; it is not a dissolution process mediated by “true
cellulose solvents”.
The supporting data and analytical evidence confirm this:
(1) The process description in SI Fig. S13 clearly states “alkaline conditions at 80°
C, with C6 participating in the reaction”, which indicates that ECH reacts mainly
with primary hydroxyls at the C6 position to form ether linkages and occasional
interchain bridges.
(2) Fig. R4 (SI Fig. S22) FTIR shows the appearance/intensification of C–O–C bands
at 1120–1160 cm⁻¹.
Fig. R4 FTIR spectra of microcrystalline cellulose (MCC) raw materials and epichlorohydrin-
modified cellulose molecules (MCC-E) via ring-opening epoxidation (Synthesis - Step 1).
(3) Fig. R5 (SI Fig. S20) ¹H NMR reveals a new signal region at 3.6–4.2 ppm.
Fig. R5 1H NMR spectra of MCC molecular raw material and epichlorohydrin-modified
cellulose molecules via ring-opening epoxidation (Synthesis - Step 1).
(4) Fig. R6 (SI Fig. S23) XRD demonstrates only a decrease in the
intensity/crystallinity of the cellulose I (002) reflection, without conversion to
cellulose II or the presence of a fully amorphous halo.
Fig. R6 XRD patterns of MCC raw materials and epichlorohydrin-modified cellulose
derivatives via ring-opening epoxidation (Synthesis - Step 1).
Taken together, these features are indicative of substitution-induced disorder, rather
than a dissolution–regeneration pathway of cellulose. The XRD changes are consistent
with the chemical “anchors” observed via FTIR/NMR and can be attributed to
etherification substitution + local crosslinking that disrupts the hydrogen-bond network,
rather than to any solvent-induced regeneration process.
Furthermore, after Step 2 (HEMA grafting), the crystalline form and overall
crystallinity of the material remain essentially unchanged (SI Fig. S25). This further
supports that the “apparent amorphisation” originates from chemical substitution and
hydrogen-bond disruption, and that no dissolution–regeneration of cellulose has
occurred.
In Step 3, the acrylamide network introduced by photocuring may induce new ordered
peaks in the XRD patterns of the DLP-printed samples (SI Fig. S12). This reflects an
increase in order associated with the final covalent network, which is not contradictory
to the “local disordering” observed in the first two steps. Instead, it represents a new
order parameter that emerges only following DLP printing and curing.
As regards the concern that “the solvent may affect all products”, we explicitly state in
the Methods section that no cellulose-dissolving solvent system was utilised in the
synthetic procedures. DMSO-d₆ was employed only as a characterisation solvent for
NMR measurements (on separately prepared samples) and was not involved in any
other synthetic pathways.

(uncured liquid CPPR resin feedstock) and CPPR-P (DLP-printed CPPR specimens).
Moreover, ECHMCC is now called MCC-E, referring to MCC molecules grafted via

5. Lines 345-346: “Moreover, the cyclic compression tests confirmed the excellent
shape memory 345 recovery function of the material (Fig. 5c).” Fig. 5c shows
nothing but pseudo-elastic (or super-elastic) behavior of CPPR material. Once
CPPR has shape memory effect, then its quasi-plastic behavior (residual strain)

Our response: We appreciate the reviewer’s observation and agree that the original
Fig. 5c demonstrated a thermal pseudo-elastic (superelastic-like) recovery under cyclic

performed additional thermally triggered shape memory experiments, and the results
are presented in the Supplementary Materials. In these new tests, the material was
programmed into a temporary shape via tensile loading and then heated to 100°C to
trigger shape recovery (Table.R3). The shape memory performance is now
quantitatively confirmed by a high shape fixity ratio (Rf), a high shape recovery ratio
(Rr), and a rapid recovery time (Tr). All these metrics demonstrate that the deformed
shape is fully fixed at room temperature and almost completely recovered upon heating.
We have also included a video in the SI showing the sample programming, shape
fixation at room temperature, and subsequent recovery upon heating, providing clear
visual evidence of the SME. All in all, we have (i) revised the text around Fig. 5c to
describe it strictly as cyclic superelastic-like recovery, and (ii) added a dedicated SME

By placing our work more clearly in the context of existing 3D-printed shape-memory
resins and comparing it with previously reported 3D-printed shape-memory systems,
we can provide a clear, specific, and integrated comparison of the research content and
conclusions, allowing us to quantitatively demonstrate the extent of the advances
achieved in this study:
(1) Comparison of “recovery rate” with FDM (thermally/magnetically triggered)
systems: FDM-printed PLA-based SMPs can achieve second-scale recovery under
external thermal or magnetic stimulation. For instance, PLA–PBAT/Fe₃O₄
nanocomposites reach >90% recovery within 3–4 s in hot-water-triggered tests (15–20 wt% Fe₃O₄),
achieving ~96–97% R within 58 s under a magnetic field (depending on composition).
r
In contrast, the CPPR resin system developed in this work rebounds spontaneously at
room temperature without any external field after an ultrahigh compressive strain of
75%, restoring both its shape and load-bearing function (strength) within 4–5 min.
This “high-load, room-temperature self-recovery” condition is not directly comparable to
FDM systems, which are mostly triggered above their T . Accordingly, the manuscript
g
emphasises the fundamental differences in load level and environmental boundary
conditions, highlighting the engineering significance of our stress-release-driven self-
recovery without external heating.
(2) Comparison of the “mechanical ceiling” with DIW green-crosslinked
nanocellulose structural components (SI Table 5): DIW, high-solids-content
nanocellulose parts employing citric acid (CA) green crosslinking followed by
esterification can reach a flexural strength and modulus of 82.78 MPa and 6.97 GPa
(ADMI 2022), respectively, while more recent DIW lignin/nanocellulose composites
achieve 102.93 MPa/9.05 GPa (ACS Omega 2024). These studies are primarily
positioned as structural materials (high strength and shape fidelity) and do not
systematically report SME metrics. In contrast, the proposed CPPR resin system
achieves a compressive strength of 115.42 MPa within a photocured network while
simultaneously combining high strength, toughness, and recoverability. By using DLP
printing, we obtain a single resin system that provides both high mechanical strength
and complex shape-memory responses, representing an advancement in coupled
performance rather than a mere competition in strength or stiffness.
(3) Comparison of manufacturability/resolution with other sustainable
photoresins: The thiolactone-based circular photoresin reported in Nature (2024)
demonstrates high-fidelity printing with 30 µm pixels, 50 µm layer thickness, and 100
µm wall thickness, demonstrating that high resolution and cross-platform
manufacturability can be achieved via sustainable chemistry routes. In this work, our
customised DLP setup achieves a minimum feature size on the order of ~5 µm,
together with efficient fabrication at a conventional 50 µm/layer and 8 s/layer. Thus,
in terms of resolution, our system is on the same order, or even finer in terms of minimum feature
size, than these state-of-the-art formulations reported in top-tier journals.
(4) Recovery mode and temperature window: The distinctive feature of the proposed
CPPR resin system is the coexistence of: (i) rapid stress-release-driven rebound at room
temperature, (ii) high load-bearing capacity and stiffness (compressive strength ≈
115.42 MPa; E_tensile ≈1.40 GPa), (iii) reproducible printing resolution and process
parameters (50 μm, 8 s per layer), and (iv) stability in aqueous environments. This
profile is complementary to most academically reported thermally triggered SMPs or
low-modulus soft networks, e.g., cardanol-based networks, E ≈ 0.2–2 MPa. Our
CPPR-P maintains a relatively high storage modulus (DMA) in the room-to-medium
temperature range (0–100°C), with a Tg of ~90°C, indicating better suitability for
structural applications at elevated service temperatures. The results indicate that, under
a “heavy-load, thick-section” condition of 75% compressive strain, the samples can
fully recover their overall shape within 4–5 min, which is an appropriate recovery
timescale for thick, load-bearing components.
The olive-oil-based system reported in AFM 2025 exhibits a Tg of around 20–25°C
(higher Tg₂) and achieves recovery within 40–100 s. It offers advantages in rapid
response for thinner parts in a mild temperature window, rendering it suitable for
constrained conditions such as biomedical use. The work published in Nat. Commun.
2023 provides a cold-programming strategy with multi-stage activatable transitions (Tc
= 62/42/<0°C), highlighting cutting-edge capabilities in programming freedom and
manufacturability of complex architectures. In this context, the proposed CPPR resin
system differs from previous studies in both the application domain and response
regime and is complementary to them.
(5) Mechanical benchmarks: In this work, a compressive strength and modulus of
115.42 MPa and 1.404 GPa, respectively, represent a rare combination of high load-
bearing capacity and recoverability among bio-based SMPs. For instance, in other
studies: the lipoate system reported in Nat. 2024 follows a circular reprinting route and
demonstrates a thermal/mechanical window comparable to commercial products, but
does not primarily target SMP metrics; the work published in Sci. Adv. 2024 presents
extreme stretchability (>1400%), but is not bio-based.
(6) Printing resolution/complexity (precision): In this work, we have achieved a
process resolution of 5 μm under DLP conditions, facilitated an integrated
demonstration of design–fabrication–performance. This resolution contrasts favourably
with the highest precision reported in comparative studies (e.g., Nat. 2024), which
involved a systematic evaluation of dimensional deviation and z-direction cure depth
at a pixel size of 30 μm. This capability highlights that our system is exceptionally well-
suited for highly customised, high-precision structural printing. It further suggests that
the established pixel/layer-thickness–to–dimensional-accuracy data from those prior
works can be leveraged for benchmarking our own high-resolution prints.
FDM relies predominantly on thermal or magnetic triggering for rapid (second-scale)
recovery, but its printing resolution and ability to form complex topologies are
inherently constrained by nozzle geometry and the layer-by-layer deposition path. DIW
systems, while excelling in strength and shape fidelity due to green-crosslinked
nanocellulose, rarely report key shape-memory effect (SME) metrics. DLP/SLA offer
advantages in resolution, complex microstructures, and scalability. Our work
demonstrates that, even when biomass is utilised as the primary feedstock, it is still
possible to achieve strength–shape-memory coupled performance on the same order as
established engineering thermosets.
From the perspective of matching materials, structures, and service conditions, CPPR
is biased toward higher service temperatures, high load-bearing capacity, and thick-
walled components, in contrast with other bio-based systems that have their own
optimal temperature windows and application scenarios and target in vivo/mild-
temperature environments with rapid response. In terms of sustainability, this study
aligns with the closed-loop remanufacturing concept reported in Nature 2024,
highlighting the potential for cyclic utilisation of cellulose segments and developing
recycle–reprint strategies (e.g., swelling/recovery and possible re-use of chain segments)
as a promising avenue for future sustainable development.

5. The authors attribute the tensile-strength increase after 100 days in water to
“hydrolysis optimizing the structure.” An alternative explanation could be
additional hydrogen bonding or physical rearrangement. To clarify the mechanism,
the authors may consider: (1) Providing stronger evidence for hydrolysis (e.g.,
FTIR, XPS, solid-state NMR, molecular weight analysis, and/or TGA); (2)
Performing control immersions in hydrogen-bonding vs. non-hydrogen-bonding
solvents and reporting the results; and/or (3) Discussing swelling behavior and
mass change during immersion.
Our response: We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to clarify the mechanism
underlying the tensile strength increase after long-term water immersion and
subsequent drying. We performed a comprehensive post-immersion analysis on printed
CPPR-P parts after 100 days in water and added the results to the SI. Jointly, the data
support a dual-mechanism: limited hydrolytic scission at accessible ester/urethane sites
plus removal of low-Mw sol fraction, followed by dry-state reinforcement via denser
H-bonding/rearrangement. This combination rationalises the observed increase in
tensile strength after drying.
Added evidences:
(1) FTIR (bulk surface, ATR): After 100 days of immersion in water and subsequent
drying, the FTIR spectra demonstrated (i) a broadened O–H band (~3200–3600
cm⁻¹) and (ii) a growth/shift of C=O features (~1700–1730 cm⁻¹) with a shoulder
consistent with –COOH/–O–C=O. However, C–O–C intensity (~1150 cm⁻¹) decreased,
consistent with mild hydrolysis and formation of more H-bond donors/acceptors in the
Fig.R6 (SI Fig. S21).
Fig. R6 FTIR analysis after immersion in water for 100 days.
(2) XPS (C1s/O1s deconvolution): The O/C ratio increased, with an enlarged O–C=O
component (~288.5 eV in C1s; ~532.5 eV in O1s), indicating again the formation
of new carboxylate/carboxylic groups by hydrolytic cleavage. Adventitious carbon
was controlled by identical cleaning/charge-ref settings in the Fig.R7 (SI Fig. S16).
Fig. R7 XPS analysis after immersion in water for 100 days.
(3) ¹H NMR (solution of extractables): The extractable fraction from aged parts
displayed new low-field methylene signals adjacent to carbonyls (≈2.2–2.5 ppm) and
a reduction of signals attributed to residual acrylate/allylic environments, evidencing
low-Mw hydrolysis fragments and further consumption of unreacted moieties in the
Fig.R8 (SI Fig. S17).
Fig. R8 1H NMR analysis after immersion in water for 100 days.
(4) GPC (extractables): The chromatogram of the post-immersion extract shifted to
lower Mn/Mw and increased in polydispersity relative to the pristine extract,
confirming chain scission in soluble tails/pendant segments while the bulk network
remained insoluble in the Fig.R9 (SI Fig. S18).
Fig. R9 GPC analysis after immersion in water for 100 days.
(5) Thermal analysis (DSC/TGA/DTG): After drying, DSC-Tg shifted upward and
ΔC_p across Tg decreased, consistent with reduced segmental mobility and higher
effective network density. Moreover, TGA (T_5%/T_onset) shifted slightly higher and
the low-T mass-loss shoulder was suppressed, indicating removal of volatiles/sol
fraction and a more thermally stable network. The char yield remained non-zero in N₂,
as expected for cellulose-derived networks in the Fig.R10 (SI Fig. S19).
