By placing our work more clearly in the context of existing 3D-printed shape-memory
resins and comparing it with previously reported 3D-printed shape-memory systems,
we can provide a clear, specific, and integrated comparison of the research content and
conclusions, allowing us to quantitatively demonstrate the extent of the advances
achieved in this study:
(1) Comparison of “recovery rate” with FDM (thermally/magnetically triggered)
systems: FDM-printed PLA-based SMPs can achieve second-scale recovery under
external thermal or magnetic stimulation. For instance, PLA–PBAT/Fe₃O₄
nanocomposites reach >90% recovery within 3–4 s in hot-water-triggered tests (15–20 wt% Fe₃O₄),
achieving ~96–97% R within 58 s under a magnetic field (depending on composition).
r
In contrast, the CPPR resin system developed in this work rebounds spontaneously at
room temperature without any external field after an ultrahigh compressive strain of
75%, restoring both its shape and load-bearing function (strength) within 4–5 min.
This “high-load, room-temperature self-recovery” condition is not directly comparable to
FDM systems, which are mostly triggered above their T . Accordingly, the manuscript
g
emphasises the fundamental differences in load level and environmental boundary
conditions, highlighting the engineering significance of our stress-release-driven self-
recovery without external heating.
(2) Comparison of the “mechanical ceiling” with DIW green-crosslinked
nanocellulose structural components (SI Table 5): DIW, high-solids-content
nanocellulose parts employing citric acid (CA) green crosslinking followed by
esterification can reach a flexural strength and modulus of 82.78 MPa and 6.97 GPa
(ADMI 2022), respectively, while more recent DIW lignin/nanocellulose composites
achieve 102.93 MPa/9.05 GPa (ACS Omega 2024). These studies are primarily
positioned as structural materials (high strength and shape fidelity) and do not
systematically report SME metrics. In contrast, the proposed CPPR resin system
achieves a compressive strength of 115.42 MPa within a photocured network while
simultaneously combining high strength, toughness, and recoverability. By using DLP
printing, we obtain a single resin system that provides both high mechanical strength
and complex shape-memory responses, representing an advancement in coupled
performance rather than a mere competition in strength or stiffness.
(3) Comparison of manufacturability/resolution with other sustainable
photoresins: The thiolactone-based circular photoresin reported in Nature (2024)
demonstrates high-fidelity printing with 30 µm pixels, 50 µm layer thickness, and 100
µm wall thickness, demonstrating that high resolution and cross-platform
manufacturability can be achieved via sustainable chemistry routes. In this work, our
customised DLP setup achieves a minimum feature size on the order of ~5 µm,
together with efficient fabrication at a conventional 50 µm/layer and 8 s/layer. Thus,
in terms of resolution, our system is on the same order, or even finer in terms of minimum feature
size, than these state-of-the-art formulations reported in top-tier journals.
(4) Recovery mode and temperature window: The distinctive feature of the proposed
CPPR resin system is the coexistence of: (i) rapid stress-release-driven rebound at room
temperature, (ii) high load-bearing capacity and stiffness (compressive strength ≈
115.42 MPa; E_tensile ≈1.40 GPa), (iii) reproducible printing resolution and process
parameters (50 μm, 8 s per layer), and (iv) stability in aqueous environments. This
profile is complementary to most academically reported thermally triggered SMPs or
low-modulus soft networks, e.g., cardanol-based networks, E ≈ 0.2–2 MPa. Our
CPPR-P maintains a relatively high storage modulus (DMA) in the room-to-medium
temperature range (0–100°C), with a Tg of ~90°C, indicating better suitability for
structural applications at elevated service temperatures. The results indicate that, under
a “heavy-load, thick-section” condition of 75% compressive strain, the samples can
fully recover their overall shape within 4–5 min, which is an appropriate recovery
timescale for thick, load-bearing components.
The olive-oil-based system reported in AFM 2025 exhibits a Tg of around 20–25°C
(higher Tg₂) and achieves recovery within 40–100 s. It offers advantages in rapid
response for thinner parts in a mild temperature window, rendering it suitable for
constrained conditions such as biomedical use. The work published in Nat. Commun.
2023 provides a cold-programming strategy with multi-stage activatable transitions (Tc
= 62/42/<0°C), highlighting cutting-edge capabilities in programming freedom and
manufacturability of complex architectures. In this context, the proposed CPPR resin
system differs from previous studies in both the application domain and response
regime and is complementary to them.
(5) Mechanical benchmarks: In this work, a compressive strength and modulus of
115.42 MPa and 1.404 GPa, respectively, represent a rare combination of high load-
bearing capacity and recoverability among bio-based SMPs. For instance, in other
studies: the lipoate system reported in Nat. 2024 follows a circular reprinting route and
demonstrates a thermal/mechanical window comparable to commercial products, but
does not primarily target SMP metrics; the work published in Sci. Adv. 2024 presents
extreme stretchability (>1400%), but is not bio-based.
(6) Printing resolution/complexity (precision): In this work, we have achieved a
process resolution of 5 μm under DLP conditions, facilitated an integrated
demonstration of design–fabrication–performance. This resolution contrasts favourably
with the highest precision reported in comparative studies (e.g., Nat. 2024), which
involved a systematic evaluation of dimensional deviation and z-direction cure depth
at a pixel size of 30 μm. This capability highlights that our system is exceptionally well-
suited for highly customised, high-precision structural printing. It further suggests that
the established pixel/layer-thickness–to–dimensional-accuracy data from those prior
works can be leveraged for benchmarking our own high-resolution prints.
FDM relies predominantly on thermal or magnetic triggering for rapid (second-scale)
recovery, but its printing resolution and ability to form complex topologies are
inherently constrained by nozzle geometry and the layer-by-layer deposition path. DIW
systems, while excelling in strength and shape fidelity due to green-crosslinked
nanocellulose, rarely report key shape-memory effect (SME) metrics. DLP/SLA offer
advantages in resolution, complex microstructures, and scalability. Our work
demonstrates that, even when biomass is utilised as the primary feedstock, it is still
possible to achieve strength–shape-memory coupled performance on the same order as
established engineering thermosets.
From the perspective of matching materials, structures, and service conditions, CPPR
is biased toward higher service temperatures, high load-bearing capacity, and thick-
walled components, in contrast with other bio-based systems that have their own
optimal temperature windows and application scenarios and target in vivo/mild-
temperature environments with rapid response. In terms of sustainability, this study
aligns with the closed-loop remanufacturing concept reported in Nature 2024,
highlighting the potential for cyclic utilisation of cellulose segments and developing
recycle–reprint strategies (e.g., swelling/recovery and possible re-use of chain segments)
as a promising avenue for future sustainable development.

5. The authors attribute the tensile-strength increase after 100 days in water to
“hydrolysis optimizing the structure.” An alternative explanation could be
additional hydrogen bonding or physical rearrangement. To clarify the mechanism,
the authors may consider: (1) Providing stronger evidence for hydrolysis (e.g.,
FTIR, XPS, solid-state NMR, molecular weight analysis, and/or TGA); (2)
Performing control immersions in hydrogen-bonding vs. non-hydrogen-bonding
solvents and reporting the results; and/or (3) Discussing swelling behavior and
mass change during immersion.
Our response: We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to clarify the mechanism
underlying the tensile strength increase after long-term water immersion and
subsequent drying. We performed a comprehensive post-immersion analysis on printed
CPPR-P parts after 100 days in water and added the results to the SI. Jointly, the data
support a dual-mechanism: limited hydrolytic scission at accessible ester/urethane sites
plus removal of low-Mw sol fraction, followed by dry-state reinforcement via denser
H-bonding/rearrangement. This combination rationalises the observed increase in
tensile strength after drying.
Added evidences:
(1) FTIR (bulk surface, ATR): After 100 days of immersion in water and subsequent
drying, the FTIR spectra demonstrated (i) a broadened O–H band (~3200–3600
cm⁻¹) and (ii) a growth/shift of C=O features (~1700–1730 cm⁻¹) with a shoulder
consistent with –COOH/–O–C=O. However, C–O–C intensity (~1150 cm⁻¹) decreased,
consistent with mild hydrolysis and formation of more H-bond donors/acceptors in the
Fig.R6 (SI Fig. S21).
Fig. R6 FTIR analysis after immersion in water for 100 days.
(2) XPS (C1s/O1s deconvolution): The O/C ratio increased, with an enlarged O–C=O
component (~288.5 eV in C1s; ~532.5 eV in O1s), indicating again the formation
of new carboxylate/carboxylic groups by hydrolytic cleavage. Adventitious carbon
was controlled by identical cleaning/charge-ref settings in the Fig.R7 (SI Fig. S16).
Fig. R7 XPS analysis after immersion in water for 100 days.
(3) ¹H NMR (solution of extractables): The extractable fraction from aged parts
displayed new low-field methylene signals adjacent to carbonyls (≈2.2–2.5 ppm) and
a reduction of signals attributed to residual acrylate/allylic environments, evidencing
low-Mw hydrolysis fragments and further consumption of unreacted moieties in the
Fig.R8 (SI Fig. S17).
Fig. R8 1H NMR analysis after immersion in water for 100 days.
(4) GPC (extractables): The chromatogram of the post-immersion extract shifted to
lower Mn/Mw and increased in polydispersity relative to the pristine extract,
confirming chain scission in soluble tails/pendant segments while the bulk network
remained insoluble in the Fig.R9 (SI Fig. S18).
Fig. R9 GPC analysis after immersion in water for 100 days.
(5) Thermal analysis (DSC/TGA/DTG): After drying, DSC-Tg shifted upward and
ΔC_p across Tg decreased, consistent with reduced segmental mobility and higher
effective network density. Moreover, TGA (T_5%/T_onset) shifted slightly higher and
the low-T mass-loss shoulder was suppressed, indicating removal of volatiles/sol
fraction and a more thermally stable network. The char yield remained non-zero in N₂,
as expected for cellulose-derived networks in the Fig.R10 (SI Fig. S19).
Fig. R10 TGA, DTG, and DSC analysis after immersion in water for 100 days.

## Paper

## Abstract

As one of the core advanced manufacturing technologies, additive manufacturing is of high
application value in the aerospace, biomedical, and industrial component manufacturing fields.
Nevertheless, current additive manufacturing materials (e.g., petroleum-based resins) face
limitations such as poor stability, limited shape recovery, and insufficient mechanical properties,
which restrict sustainable manufacturing progress. Inspired by the stress-dissipation mechanism in
plant cell walls, we develop a cellulose-based photopolymerizable resin that delivers exceptional
stiffness-deformability synergy and spatiotemporally shape memory capability. These structures
integrate excellent mechanical strength and rapid recovery performance after deformation. The
additive manufacturing cellulose-based photopolymerizable resin material exhibits a synergistic
stiffness-deformability profile, achieving a compressive strength of 115.42 MPa and stiffness of
1404.16 MPa. These characteristics lay the foundation for specialized defense components, energy
absorption systems, and spatiotemporal memory materials.

---

## Introduction

Additive manufacturing (AM), also known as 3D printing, represents one of pivotal
component fabrication methodologies in contemporary industry and constitutes a critically
prioritized technology for future industrial development1-3. AM enables materials to achieve
architected geometries, multifunctional integration, and intelligent responses, exhibiting
exceptional compatibility with rapidly advancing sectors such as aerospace, defense machinery,
and biomedical manufacturing4,5. Contemporary AM materials principally comprise brittle
polymers and rigid photopolymers, and despite their substantial stiffness, their toughness and
deformation capacity are inadequate6-10. Consequently, post-printed components undergo
irreversible deformation under load-induced damage, compromising their functionality and
reducing their service lifetime7,11,12. The annual waste volume of discarded AM products has
reached substantial levels with a persistent upward trend, posing serious challenges to material
utilization efficiency and environmental sustainability. In this context, developing high-strength
AM materials that combine rigid structural integrity with shape memory (flexible) performance
and rapid recovery capabilities remains a critical scientific challenge.

Cellulose constitutes the most abundant biomass resource in Earth's natural systems, offering
the advantages of renewability, ubiquitous availability, and low-cost sourcing13. At the same time,
the energy dissipation mechanism in plant cell walls - particularly through dynamic cellulose
microfibril sliding - serves as the fundamental strategy that enables plants to withstand external
mechanical stresses while maintaining structural toughness and environmental resilience14,15.
According to current research, cellulose has been primarily employed in digital light processing
(DLP)-AM materials as blended filler or minor additive. Previous studies on 3D printing of
biomass and its derivatives have shown that nanocellulose can be esterified with green small
molecules (e.g., citric acid) or blended with lignin and related components, thereby enabling direct
ink writing (DIW) printing of high-solids-content (≥25 wt%) structural parts with high strength
and good shape retention (flexural strength of 83–149 MPa and flexural modulus of 7–15 G Pa).16-
20 In contrast, in this work cellulose is used as the primary carbon source to directly synthesize
photocurable resins suitable for DLP printing (rather than aqueous paste-type DIW). While
maintaining high mechanical performance, these resins impart pronounced shape-memory
behavior and multi-cycle anti-fatigue capability to the printed structures, thereby overcoming the
limitations of existing DIW structural materials in terms of being “photopatternable, rapidly
formable, and capable of programmable deformation”.

Through mechanism-guided design that replicates the morphological preservation and stress
resilience mechanisms of natural plant cellulose. In plant cell walls, semi-disordered lamellar
architectures enable cellulose microfibrils to slide controllably through dynamic hydrogen bond
rupture and reconfiguration under external mechanical stress21-25. This hierarchical energy
dissipation mechanism effectively converts mechanical energy into thermal dissipation or other
non-destructive forms while maintaining structural integrity26-28. Tai4 and Zhang5 experimentally
demonstrated that cellulose microfibrils are the primary stress-bearing components during plant
cell wall deformation. Their work revealed that semi-disordered lamellar layers facilitate confined
cellulose microfibril sliding, which serves as the dominant energy dissipation mechanism in plant
cellular systems. This dynamic sliding behavior critically determines both the elastic-plastic
transition characteristics and deformation recovery thresholds of cell walls under multiaxial
loading conditions5,29.

Inspired by this dynamic mechanism, this paper designs a cellulose-derived photopolymer
network to achieve optimal balance between rigidity and flexibility in AM materials (Fig. 1). The
analysis reveals that under external forces, the semi-disordered microfiber network undergoes
loosening of intermolecular hydrogen bonds, enabling limited sliding that dissipates energy and
maintains morphological or structural stability. Furthermore, the synthesis of a photocurable resin
containing photosensitive groups capable of radical polymerization is presented. In particular, the
photocurable resin is synthesized using microcrystalline cellulose as the raw material through a
two-step reaction involving epichlorohydrin grafting and hydroxyethyl methacrylate (HEMA)
substitution. Using acrylamide as a crosslinking framework, the resin can be rapidly printed via
DLP at 5-10 s/layer. The resulting material combines a rigid carbon-chain framework with a
dynamically responsive cellulose-entangled structure, achieving an excellent rigidity-flexibility
balance. The AM cellulose-based photopolymerizable resin (CPPR-P) material exhibits
exceptional performance: high compressive strength (115.42 MPa), high elastic modulus (1404.16
MPa), and excellent mechanical cycling durability. In addition, it demonstrates outstanding shape
memory functionality, rapidly recovering its original state under both unidirectional stress (vertical
compression) and multi-directional stress (bus rolling) tests. This stiffness-deformability
synergistic material fulfills the demand in advanced applications for materials that simultaneously
offer high mechanical strength and superior damage-mitigating shape memory capabilities.

---

## Results

Spatiotemporal memory and compressive properties of cellulose-based photopolymerizable resin
(CPPR). To meet diverse application requirements, AM resin must achieve high-precision rapid
printing of materials that can simultaneously resist both orderly uniaxial stresses and complex
multiaxial stresses while maintaining spatiotemporal memory capabilities for rapid recovery after
deformation induced by destructive external stresses30-34.

A 3D mechanical support structure of CPPR was designed and fabricated via DLP printing
(Fig. 2a), exhibiting well-defined geometric features and pristine architecture. A universal
mechanical tester (Fig. 2a) capable of generating uniform uniaxial stress and a large vehicle (bus;
Fig. 2b) with irregular multidirectional stress were used to simulate material stress and recovery
in different scenarios. During controlled uniaxial compression testing, the specimens were
compressed to their ultimate compressive state (75% strain). Upon release, they achieved rapid
structural and morphological recovery within 4-5 min. Throughout the compression-recovery
cycles (Movie S1), The CPPR-P demonstrated dynamic stress-adaptive behavior under overload
conditions while maintaining structural integrity without catastrophic failure. Under dynamic bus
loading (Movie S2), which generated disordered multidirectional stresses, specimens were
positioned directly in the wheel path to ensure full compressive traversal. After compression, the
3D mechanical support structure retained their mechanical support functionality while rapidly
recovering both morphology and architectural integrity. It should be noted that throughout the
model design, slicing, and DLP printing processes, high-fidelity rapid fabrication was achieved
without requiring auxiliary support structures. This demonstrates that the synergistic compatibility
between the CPPR resin material and optimized DLP printing parameters effectively streamlines
manufacturing workflows while significantly improving material efficiency and manufacturing
throughput.

The excellent mechanical strength and spatiotemporal memory capability of the 3D
mechanical support structure, combining rigidity with flexibility, depend highly on four factors: (i)
the limited sliding of the cellulose chains in the cured molecular structure, (ii) the dynamic fracture
and recombination of loose intermolecular hydrogen bonds under external stress, (iii) the rigid
carbon-chain skeleton formed by C=C bond reactions, and (iv) the multi-scale synergistic effects
between microphase-separated structures (Fig. 2c). Following the mechanism-guided design
cellulose-based photopolymerizable resin, precise layer-by-layer control of micro-nano level
curing is achieved via DLP printing. This enables precise structural and property control,
optimizing functional the characteristics of the material.

To characterize the compressive mechanical properties of CPPR-P, uniaxial compression tests
were conducted on a universal testing machine under different loading regimes. Herein, multiple
printable materials were fabricated: CPPR, a hydroxyethyl methacrylate-based
photopolymerizable resin without cellulose (HEMA-PR), and non-epoxidized CPPR (NE-CPPR).
Following GB/T 1041-2008 and its referenced standards, multiple cylindrical and prismatic
specimen sets were prepared and tested to obtain mean mechanical property values via replicated
experiments. Under uniaxial compression testing (Fig. 2d), the CPPR-P specimens demonstrated
exceptional mechanical performance, achieving a compressive strength of 115.42 MPa. Moreover,
CPPR-P exhibited an extended elastic regime (strain of ~80%), with complete deformation
recovery upon stress unloading and no permanent damage. These quantitative findings align with
the compressive recovery behavior observed in the 3D mechanical support structure (Fig. 2a,
Movie S1). During cyclic compression testing at 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% strain amplitudes (Fig.
2e), all CPPR-P specimens rapidly stabilized into steady-state responses, exhibiting significant
energy dissipation and cyclic stability, which are critical characteristics for shape-memory
functionality and recovery performance. In addition, CPPR-P achieved dynamic stability in energy
dissipation within each cycle (Fig. 2f), with no observable strain softening across different strain
conditions. This indicates that CPPR-P has consistent recovery and shape-memory capabilities
over a broad strain range.

Tensile properties, curing process, and simulation results. In conventional photocured AM resins,
the crosslinking/curing degree and mechanical strength increase with photoinitiator concentration
and light exposure time. This relationship applies also to the CPPR photocured resin, which can
rapidly generate radicals and undergo crosslinking polymerization after reaction initiation, curing
rapidly within 5-10 s. Samples made of CPPR, HEMA-PR, and NE-CPPR were prepared and
uniaxial tensile tests were conducted under different loading conditions using a universal
mechanical testing machine (Fig. 3a). In cyclic tensile tests (Fig. 3b), the CPPR-P samples
exhibited a low-damage behavior dominated by elastic deformation, with clear energy absorption
and shape recovery. It was observed that after multi-cycle tension, samples remained in the elastic
stage with no structural damage. On the other hand, the printing sample of NE-CPPR entered the
plastic buckling stage after the first cycle, undergoing permanent damage. Moreover, the printing
sample of NE-CPPR exhibited significant strain softening and high energy dissipation during
cyclic stretching, indicating limited deformation recovery capability and poor fatigue resistance.
While the printing sample of HEMA-PR completely lacked cyclic recovery functionality, CPPR-
P demonstrated superior performance in terms of the maximum stress it could reach across
successive cycles (Fig. 3c). In multiple cyclic tests, CPPR-P stress could be maintained at nearly
100%, indicating its excellent cyclic recovery performance and fatigue resistance. In contrast,
HEMA-PR and NE-CPPR underwent rapid structural failure during the cyclic process and lost
their mechanical strength.

Tensile strength testing (Fig. 3d) revealed nonlinear stress-strain behavior in all specimens,
with distinct loading/unloading hysteresis loops indicative of significant energy absorption. Here,
the tensile strength of CPPR-P reached 25.16 MPa, significantly higher than that of the printing
sample of NE-CPPR (4.55 MPa). Although the tensile strength of the printing sample of HEMA-
PR was as high as 27.71 MPa, it lacked cyclic recovery capability due to its highly rigid and brittle
structure. The printing sample of HEMA-PR can be slightly stronger at first pull, but brittle and
non-recoverable; CPPR-P achieves engineering-level strength and repeatable recovery due to its
cellulose-based photopolymerizable resin—this is why, for functional AM components, CPPR is
the more suitable material despite a modest Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS) difference. The elastic
moduli of CPPR-P, printing sample of HEMA-PR and NE-CPPR were 1404.16 MPa, 1412.96
MPa, and 12.30 MPa, respectively (Fig. 3e). CPPR-P environmental adaptability (water-resistance)
was also assessed by completely immersing a sample in water for 100 days, and observing the
entire process (Fig. S1). Interestingly, throughout the 100-day immersion period, the CPPR-P
maintained its morphology and volume without exhibiting any significant changes. Furthermore,
the mechanical properties of CPPR-P immersed in water for 0, 50, and 100 days were determined.
According to the results (Fig. S2), the tensile strength of CPPR-P at days 0, 50, and 100 was 25.16
MPa, 22.55 MPa, and 42.94 MPa, respectively, demonstrating excellent water resistance. After 50
days of immersion, the tensile strength of CPPR-P remained similar to that of day 0, exhibiting
typical nonlinear stress-strain behavior and cyclic recovery capability. Remarkably, after 100 days
of immersion, the tensile strength unexpectedly doubled, which can be attributed to water-induced
secondary crosslinking and network densification. During this process, selective hydrolysis
optimizes the structure by breaking weak bonds and retaining strong ones. At the same time,
cellulose microfibrils undergo orientation-enhanced sliding followed by failure processes (Fig. S2
and Fig. S3). Nonetheless, at this point, CPPR-P exhibited an extremely short elastic stage, and the
slope of the linear segment was extremely high (indicating significant brittleness), suggesting
complete loss of deformation recovery capability. Even after such a long immersion period, CPPR-
P stiffness (Young’s modulus) remained almost unchanged: 1404.16 MPa on Day 0, 1202.47 MPa
on Day 50, and 1586.19 MPa on Day 100 (Fig. S3).

Uniaxial tensile testing was simulated along the X-X orientation to quantitatively capture the
steady-state stress-strain response via computational modeling (Fig. 3f). According to the
simulation results, the cured CPPR exhibited a tensile strength of 27.80 MPa and strain of 28.10%
along the X-X direction. These computational predictions agreed well with the experimental
measurements (25.16 MPa tensile strength), empirically substantiating the validity of the
established theoretical framework and research conclusions. Concurrently, the simulated sample
density stabilized at 1.19 g/cm³ (Fig. S4), exhibiting close agreement with the experimental one
(1.14 g/cm³).

In the photoinitiated radical polymerization process, 2,4,6-trimethylbenzoyl-
diphenylphosphine oxide (TPO) served as the photoinitiator to drive the polymerization reaction
(Fig. 3g). TPO dosage affects the concentration of subsequently generated free radicals, which in
turn controls the free-radical polymerization rate, the crosslinking degree in the final material, and
material uniformity and density35. Under ultraviolet (UV) irradiation at 405 nm, TPO undergoes
homolysis to form benzoyl and diphenylphosphinyl radicals. These radicals attack the monomer
double bonds (R1 and R2) in CPPR and acrylamide, initiating chain polymerization and forming
polymer chains. The HEMA-dominated rigid polymer backbone provides pronounced stiffness but
introduces inherent brittleness, thereby deteriorating strain recovery capacity—as evidenced by
HEMA-PR experimental results. Conversely, cellulose molecular chains form a crosslinked
network architecture that enables confined sliding, thereby overcoming this limitation and
endowing the material with synergistic stiffness-deformability properties. According to the
simulation results of the CPPR free-radical polymerization crosslinking reaction (Fig. 3h), under
DLP-printing-like conditions, the polymerization achieves stable crosslinked network formation
with controlled conversion kinetics.

Shear and rheological tests. Beyond providing exceptional control over compressive and tensile
properties, DLP printing further facilitates precise modulation of CPPR shear response and
rheological behavior. This capability enhances dimensional accuracy in complex architectures,
interlayer fusion quality, and dynamic load-bearing performance under operational stress
conditions. In AM, the rheological properties of materials affect not only structural precision and
interlayer bonding but also material stability and post-printing strength via microstructure
regulation. In addition, mechanical shear strength directly reflects interlayer adhesion, which is
critical for materials operating under interface stress conditions. The investigation and
optimization of these properties have advanced photopolymerization AM for manufacturing high-
precision complex structures.

In the present study, shear tests were conducted under different loading regimes using a
universal testing machine (Fig. 4a). Under shear stress loading, both CPPR and HEMA-PR printed
samples exhibited evident elastic stages and yield points (CPPR: 7%; HEMA-PR: 6%), indicating
that the material was in the linear elastic deformation stage and underwent reversible elastic
deformation under external forces (Fig. 4b). The shear strength values of CPPR-P, the printing
sample of HEMA-PR and NE-CPPR were 25.83 MPa, 25.30 MPa, and 2.47 MPa, respectively
(Fig. 4c). The CPPR-P exhibited a distinct yield plateau (7-10% strain) after reaching the yield
point, during which cellulose-mediated molecular chain sliding (microplastic flow) occurred,
enabling continuous stress dissipation and release. On the other hand, post-yielding, the printing
sample of HEMA-PR immediately entered the plastic deformation stage (brittle failure stage). The
printing sample of NE-CPPR sample exhibited a plateau region with shear stress values close to
zero, suggesting fluid-like behavior characteristics. Another intuitive expression of shear
performance is the maximum yield stress. A higher yield stress enables structural integrity
preservation under shear loading (CPPR: 2651.02 N;HEMA-PR: 2726.06 N; NE-CPPR: 237.60
N) (Fig.S5). Overall, CPPR-P demonstrated excellent shear performance, with high shear strength,
peak yield stress, and fracture strain, achieving an optimal strength-toughness balance under shear
conditions.

To evaluate the rheo-structural properties, the rheological behavior of both DLP-printed CPPR
cylindrical specimens and the cellulose-based photocurable print resin liquid (CPPR-L) was
characterized. The rheological test results for the DLP-printed CPPR cylindrical samples (Fig. 4d)
revealed that the initial storage modulus (G'), loss modulus (G''), and complex viscosity (η*)
reached first a high yield plateau (0-10% strain) with increasing shear load. Upon exceeding the
critical shear blocking strain, all three parameters exhibited a gradual degradation. It can be
observed that the G' and G'' values of CPPR-P remained high over a wide range of shear strains,
demonstrating superior stiffness and stability under varied deformation conditions. In addition, the
intersection point of G' and G'', i.e., the point where the storage and loss moduli are equal, occurred
at higher shear strains in CPPR-P, confirming its wide elastic deformation range. The rheological
tests of CPPR-L (Fig. S6) revealed that the viscosity decreased gradually with increasing shear
rate, indicating a gentle shear-thinning behavior. This smooth viscosity reduction enhances
printing stability by maintaining optimal flowability while minimizing printing defects caused by
abrupt viscosity fluctuations. Furthermore, CPPR resin demonstrated viscosity stability across a
wide range of shear rates, which helps preserve the dimensional accuracy and shape fidelity of
printed parts, especially during multi-layer printing of intricate and complex structures.

Comparison of CPPR resin characteristics and properties before and after AM solidification with
other mainstream materials. To verify the industrial applicability of AM CPPR materials with
synergistic stiffness-deformability characteristics, comprehensive multi-dimensional performance
evaluation under operational conditions remains essential. To this end, comprehensive
comparative studies on CPPR-P, UV-curable epoxy resin (UVEP), polyamide nylon (PA), and
thermoplastic polyurethane elastomer (TPU) were conducted. These evaluations included ultimate
compression recovery (shape-memory function), compressive strength, cyclic compression,
tensile strength, and cyclic tension tests, as well as comparative analysis of material stiffness
(elastic modulus). In the compression recovery test (Fig. 5a and Movie S3 and S4), the 3D
mechanical support structure of CPPR manufactured via AM was compressed to the maximum
deformation state. The 3D mechanical support structure was able to quickly recover its shape and
morphology within 4-5 min after stress release. Conversely, during the initial testing phase, the
UVEP specimen underwent abrupt structural fragmentation upon stress application, exhibiting
catastrophic fracture that excluded any recovery potential. Although PA maintained partial
structural integrity during the experiment, its structure failed after it was compressed to its
maximum deformation state, leading to permanent deformation. After stress release, PA lost its
shape memory and recovery functions. Lastly, TPU proved unsuitable for fabricating the 3D
mechanical support structures required in this study via AM.

In the comparative assessment of compressive strength (Fig. 5b), CPPR-P demonstrated
significantly superior performance, achieving an exceptional 115.42 MPa, outperforming UVEP
(86.79 MPa), PA (49.02 MPa), and TPU (1.89 MPa). This indicates that CPPR-P can withstand
higher external stresses while maintaining structural integrity. Moreover, the cyclic compression
tests confirmed the excellent cyclic reversible elasticity at room temperature of the material (Fig.
5c). During repeated cyclic compression tests, CPPR-P consistently maintained a distinct elastic
behavior without structural failure, maintaining full specimen extension and recovery across all
loading/unloading cycles. The unique shape memory property of CPPR-
P is also absent from other materials. We obtain Shape fixation rate (Rf) = 60.5% ± 4.6%, Shape
recovery rate (Rr) = 94.5% ± 2.5%, and Trigger/switch temperature (t_r) ≈ 60–70 s at 100 °C.
No sample fractured during programming or recovery. (Table S1 “Shape-memory tests” and Movie
S5) In contrast, TPU exhibited a pronounced strain-softening behavior, which can be attributed to
interfacial debonding and internal crack initiation and propagation, leading to gradual recovery
capacity degradation. Meanwhile, neither UVNEP nor PA demonstrated any measurable cyclic
recovery capacity. These characteristics are clearly evidenced in the cyclic compression energy
dissipation profiles (Fig. 5d), where CPPR-P rapidly stabilizes into a consistent energy dissipation
plateau. Furthermore, the stiffness of CPPR-P (elastic modulus: 1404.16 MPa) maintained a
significant advantage over PA (650.08 MPa) and TPU (37.31 MPa), while being comparable to
UVEP (1418.05 MPa) (Fig. S7 and S8). CPPR-P demonstrated exceptional energy dissipation
capacity and cyclic recovery performance in both tensile testing (Fig. S9) and cyclic tensile energy
dissipation profiles (Fig. S10). Overall, the excellent mechanical strength and cyclic recovery
performance of CPPR resin significantly broaden its potential real-life applications while
improving its service life and reducing usage costs.

Subsequently, other important properties of CPPR-P were characterized and analyzed to
investigate and determine its applicability and stability over a wide application field range.
Through structural composition characterization, the reaction mechanism and memory recovery
function of CPPR-P were validated. Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA; Fig. 5e) revealed the
loss-modulus maximum near ~90 °C (≈Tg) indicates the primary α-relaxation of the crosslinked
network, indicating the superior mechanical energy storage and elastic performance of CPPR-P
below 100°C. The loss modulus (E'') peak at 90°C (near Tg) signified maximum energy dissipation
through molecular chain relaxation and sliding, indicative of crosslinked network homogeneity.
Consistent with a load-bearing covalent network with restricted segmental mobility. Furthermore,
the peak magnitude of the loss factor (tanδ) reflects the energy dissipation capacity of CPPR-P. Its
prominent peak at TG transition demonstrates exceptional damping performance, rendering it
suitable for vibration attenuation and energy-absorbing applications.

Thermal analyses via differential scanning calorimetry (DSC; Fig. 5f) and derivative
thermogravimetric analysis (DTG; Fig. 5g) revealed the exceptional thermal stability of CPPR-P,
with onset decomposition temperatures above 250°C. Tg shifts upward and ΔCp across Tg
decreases after curing, evidencing reduced chain mobility and higher network density; the
transition width remains moderate, suggesting a reasonably homogeneous network rather than a
broad phase mixture.

Furthermore, scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Fig. S11) and X-ray diffraction (XRD; Fig.
S12) analyses of AM-fabricated CPPR-P sample interfaces revealed a homogeneous dense and
stable microstructure. These observations confirm the exceptional printability and process
compatibility of CPPR resin in AM, directly explaining its demonstrated outstanding mechanical
strength and shape memory performance.

Other, CPPR-P absorbs water but retains integrity and reaches a plateau swelling of ≈ 26–
29 % ( Swelling test; Table S2), indicative of a densely crosslinked acrylate–cellulose network
with limited free volume. The modest ≈ 17 % mass loss after 48 h likely reflects extraction of
residual oligomers/sol fractions plus minor hydrolysis of ester linkages near the surface
(Hydrolytic mass-loss; Table S3); the absence of disintegration corroborates the robust covalent
crosslink density.

Together with our mechanical data, these results support CPPR-P as a water-stable, high-
strength photoresin suitable for printed parts operating in humid/aqueous environments. These
results confirm that the CPPR resin crosslinked network is water-stable (no disintegration) while
allowing controlled water uptake, consistent with its covalent network plus reversible H-bonding.

## Methods

Materials. Microcrystalline cellulose was purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical
Technology Co., Ltd. Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), epichlorohydrin (ECH), sodium hydroxide
particles, hydroxyethyl methacrylate (HEMA), acrylamide, and ethylene glycol diacrylate
(EGDMA) were all purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. Ultra-
pure water was prepared in our laboratory. N, N'-Methylene Bisacrylamide (MBA) was purchased
from Tianjin Guangfu Fine Chemical Research Institute, while (2,4,6-trimethylbenzoyl)
diphenylphosphine oxide (TPO) was purchased from Shanghai Titan Scientific Co., Ltd.

Product synthesis and characterization. The supplementary material includes detailed synthesis
procedures and characterization data for the polymer, including reaction equations, spectra
analyses, and chromatograms.

Synthesis – Step 1 the prepared process of MCC epichlorohydrin (Fig. S13). First, an epoxide ring-opening
reaction occurs between the cellulose chains and epichlorohydrin. Briefly, 2 g of pretreated microcrystalline
cellulose (MCC) was swollen and uniformly dispersed in 70 mL of DMSO and maintained at 50 °C in a water
bath until a homogeneous suspension was obtained. Epichlorohydrin (40 mL) was then placed in a dropping
funnel and added dropwise at a rate of 10 mL h⁻¹. Subsequently, 15 mL of 30 wt% aqueous NaOH solution was
added dropwise over 30–45 min using a dropping funnel. The mixture was then heated to 80–85 °C and allowed
to react for a further 4 h. After cooling the reaction system to room temperature, the functionalized MCC
precursor was obtained. Under alkaline conditions at 80 °C, the epoxide group of epichlorohydrin undergoes a
ring-opening reaction to generate reactive sites, at which point the primary hydroxyl group at the C6 position of
cellulose reacts with it. The resulting product is named as MCC-E. After completion of the epichlorohydrin
ring-opening grafting, the key workup objective is to eliminate residual epichlorohydrin, which is volatile. The
reaction mixture is cooled to room temperature and the remaining epichlorohydrin is removed by rotary
evaporation (Vacuum degree 220-250Pa, 75 ℃, rotation speed 20, time 45 minutes) under reduced pressure
until a constant mass (or no further condensate) is observed. This step effectively prevents carryover of unreacted
ECH into Step 2 and ensures safe handling and reproducibility.

Synthesis – Step 2 the synthetic of Cellulose-based photopolymerisable resin (CPPR) precursor (Fig. S14). On
the basis of the precursor obtained in Step 1, free-radical photoreactive groups were grafted onto the cellulose
backbone. The product from Step 1 was transferred into a 500 mL round-bottom flask, and 0.5 wt%
methanesulfonic acid (CH₃SO₃H) was used as a catalyst. Then, 50 wt% hydroxyethyl methacrylate (HEMA)
(C₆H₁₀O₃) was added to introduce the free-radical photoreactive grafting groups, and the mixture was stirred at
70 °C in a water bath for 6 h. After completion of the reaction, the system was cooled to 50 °C and maintained
for a further 4 h to ensure complete conversion. The resulted product is cellulose-based photopolymerizable resin
(CPPR) precursor used for DLP additive manufacturing. After the HEMA grafting reaction, the workup aims to
remove (i) unreacted HEMA and (ii) the acid catalyst. We accomplish this by a combination of reduced-pressure
rotary evaporation (Vacuum degree 500-600Pa, 60 ℃, rotation speed 20, time 60-90 minutes) (to remove
residual HEMA) and neutralization (Add triethylamine dropwise at room temperature (1.05 equivalents relative
to the acid), and stir for 10-15 minutes, to quench the acid catalyst. And the mixture was passed through a short
plug of basic alumina to capture the residual acid /salts.), followed by brief vacuum treatment to remove trace
volatiles.

Synthesis – Step 3 the synthetic of cellulose-based photocurable print resin liquid (CPPR-L) (Fig. S15). The
reaction namely the photo-initiated free-radical polymerization of the CPPR resin. First, 150 mL of the above-
prepared CPPR resin monomer was transferred into a 500 mL round-bottom flask, and 15 mL of “ethylene glycol
dimethacrylate (EGDMA)” was added as a reactive co-monomer for the subsequent free-radical polymerization.
The mixture was stirred at 50 °C until complete dissolution. Afterward, the temperature was lowered to 30 °C
(to avoid premature partial polymerization caused by excessive temperature), and 40 wt% acrylamide (C₃H₅NO)
was added as a crosslinker, The reaction was allowed to proceed with stirring at 30 °C for 30 min. Subsequently,
0.1 wt% N,N′-methylenebisacrylamide (MBA) was introduced, and the mixture was stirred for another 30 min.
Finally, 0.5 wt% TPO was added as the photoinitiator, and stirring was continued until a homogeneous cellulose-
based photocurable print resin liquid (CPPR-L) capable of undergoing UV-induced free-radical polymerization
was obtained. The CPPR-L2 and CPPR-L3 were fabricated according to the different contents of CPPR and
acrylamide. HEMA-PR refers to photocurable print resin only with HEMA. NE-CPPR refers to CPPR without
MCC epichlorohydrin step. Removal of extractables and ensuring full cure: Step 3 produces a photocurable resin
by formulation; therefore, “product purification” relevant to materials testing is performed on the printed parts.
The as-printed objects are washed in anhydrous ethanol to remove unreacted/soluble residues at the surface,
followed by 405 nm & 5min post-curing to drive conversion to completion before characterization.

Description of the components of various resins used in this work (Table S4).

DLP additive manufacturing. A MiiCraft Ultra 150 3D printer was used for AM using the CPPR
material. The DLP parameters were set as follows: layer thickness of 50 μm, exposure time per
layer of 8 s, five base layers with an exposure time of 13 s, five buffer layers, and light-machine
power of 7.5 mW·cm⁻². After printing, the samples were placed in anhydrous ethanol to remove
excess liquid resin and then stabilized in a UV curing chamber (405 nm) for 5 min. The resulted
product is named CPPR-P.

The detailed printing parameters for the other resin formulations used in this work are summarized
in the table S5.

Characterization

NMR Spectroscopy. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy was conducted using a
Bruker AVANCE III 500 MHz NMR spectrometer. The samples were dissolved in deuterated
dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO-d6) for 10 min. The mixture was cooled to room temperature and then
filtered through a 0.45-μm filter membrane to obtain a clear filtrate suitable for NMR studies.

FTIR spectroscopy. Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy was performed using a
WQF-510A spectrometer in attenuated total reflectance (ATR) mode. FTIR spectra were acquired
across the infrared range (4000–400 cm⁻¹) with 32 scans per sample.

XRD. X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was performed using a Shimadzu 6100 diffractometer to
identify the characteristic peaks and determine material crystallinity. The scanning parameters
were: angular range of 5°–65° (2θ); scan rate of 4° min⁻¹.

GPC. Gel permeation chromatography (GPC) was performed with an Agilent PL GPC50
instrument. GPC measurements were carried out on the soluble extractable fraction of the printed
samples using deuterated DMSO as the mobile phase (GPC measurements were performed on the
DMSO-soluble (extractable) fraction of the printed samples, rather than the entire crosslinked
network). The mass concentration of the test solution was 0.10 mg mL-1, the test volume was 100.0
μL, the flow rate was 1.0 mL min-1, and the column temperature was 40°C. DMSO (DMSO-d₆ in
our measurements) was used to dissolve the extractables and as the eluent.

Micro-morphology analysis. The surface morphology of the samples was observed and studied
via scanning electron microscopy (SEM; HT7800, Hitachi, Japan) in secondary electron mode
with an acceleration voltage of 20.0 kV.

Dynamic thermal performance analysis. Thermogravimetry-differential scanning calorimetry
(TG-DSC) analysis was performed using a Netzsch STA 449 F3 simultaneous thermal analyzer to
assess the dynamic thermal behavior of samples before and after AM. Specimens weighing 5-8 mg
were heated from 20°C to 800°C under nitrogen atmosphere at a controlled heating rate of 20
K·min⁻¹. Baseline correction was conducted by constructing pre- and post-transition baselines
(linear segments) and subtracting instrumental drift; second heating scan is shown after the first
heat/cool cycle to remove thermal history.

Dynamic mechanical analysis. The glass transition temperature, storage modulus, loss modulus,
and loss factor curves of the samples were obtained using a Q800 dynamic mechanical analyzer
(TA Instruments). Measurements were conducted under nitrogen atmosphere over the temperature
range of 25°C-500°C, with a heating rate of 10°C min−1 and frequency of 1 Hz.

Rheological performance testing. The rheological properties, such as storage modulus (elastic
modulus) G', loss modulus G'', loss factor tan δ, and complex viscosity, of the CPPR materials
before and after AM were assessed using a HAAKE MARS60 rheometer. Tests were conducted at
room temperature with a shear rate range of 0.01-1000 s-1.

Mechanical performance testing. An electronic universal testing machine (SHIMADZU AGS-
X 10kN) was used to determine the mechanical properties of the AM CPPR samples. Tests
included cyclic compression, compressive strength, cyclic tensile strength, tensile strength, and
shear performance measurements. Five replicates were tested for each condition, with reported
values representing averages. The tensile specimen used dumbbell shaped standard specimens
(thickness: 2mm; width: 4mm; gauge length: 50mm), and the compression and shear specimens
used rectangular standard specimens (length: 10mm; width: 10mm; height: 25mm), with a testing
rate of 10mm/min.

Swelling test. DLP-printed CPPR bars (rectangular, same geometry as mechanical tests) were

performed using Materials Studio (Version 2023, Dassault Systèmes). Initial reactant models were

Subsequently, the crosslinking and curing reactions were simulated (Temperature: 298 K; Pressure:

the crosslinking degree, ring penetration, and molecular structure to verify the reaction progress

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

Zhao et al., in the revised manuscript entitled “Additive manufacturing of biomimetic biomass-derived materials with excellent mechanical performance and shape memory” [Manuscript ID: NCOMMS-25-54659-T], present and interesting approach to develop new photocrosslinkable materials with improved sustainability using cellulose derivatives. The manuscript builds upon the authors hypothesis that plant cell walls dissipative mechanism can be explored to create bio-inspired materials with superior mechanical properties.

The study is interesting and the research, analysis and synthetic work is certainly, of interest to a large readership. While the manuscript presents an interesting approach to the research question, there are significant scientific issues that need to be thoroughly addressed to meet the standards expected by a journal of this level.

1) There are critical methodological details missing. One of them is the synthetic route towards the obtainment of the photocurable resin. Figures 9, 10 and 11 from SI do not provide sufficient detail to allow the reproduction of the reaction. This information should be added to the manuscript.
2) The characterization of the precursors (by both FTIR and NMR) does not allow the confirmation of the functionalization of the MCC precursor. What was the calculated degree of substitution of the polymeric precursor? 13 C NMR can be provided useful information.
3) What is the constitution of the uncured CPPR liquid resin (UC-CPPR)? Does it already contain the AM monomers mentioned in line 95? If so, the conclusions provided on Figure 17 from SI should be revised.
4) The description of the resins used in this work should be also added. A table describing the amounts of each component on the resins (photoinitiator, MCC precursor, AM and crosslinker) must be provided in the manuscript.
5) The DLP parameters should be provided with more detail. Was it the same for all the samples? What does a power of 125% means using standard irradiation units (mW/cm2)?
6) The lattice 3D model used to print the samples should be added to SI.
6) The nomenclature CPPR, HMPR and NE-CPPR is somewhat confusion. What does HPMR and NE-CPPR stand for?
Lines 156 and 157 provide some information, but more details are needed.
7) From Figure 3d, it is possible to confirm the superior performance of HMPR in comparison with CPPR. The authors should elaborate more on this topic and provide more details about the composition of the HMPR resin.
8) Swelling and hydrolytic degradation studies should be added.
9) Figure 4c) considering the details, the viscosity seems too high for a DLP printing process. Weren’t there problems of printing resolution?
10) How were the comparison standards (UVEP, PA and TPU) prepared? Also by DLP processes?
11) DMA, DSC and TGA studies should be all revised.
12) What tested in DMA, a printed sample or the resin? Which geometry was used? Data presented in Figure 5e does not match with what is described in lines 555 to 559.
13) In Figure 21 from SI. What is the explanation for such a high weight remaining at 800ºC?
14) Data from GPC should also be revised. Which solvent was used for the analysis? Were printed samples analyzed as stated in Figure 22 from SI?

### Reviewer 2

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

### Reviewer 3

This paper reports a cellulose-based photopolymerizable resin (CPPR) with exceptional stiffness-deformability synergy and spatiotemporal shape memory capabilities. A bionic structure design approach was proposed, which transforms brittle photocurable 3D-printing materials into bio-inspired structures. This paper carries interesting results. However, there are some concerns regarding the synthesis of CPPR and its characteristics.

1. Lines 64-67: The authors said, “However, the potential of using cellulose as a primary feedstock for directly synthesizing high-performance printable materials remains either unexplored or results in products with compromised mechanical and functional properties.” They did not recognize that nanocellulose has been 3D printed for structural materials by esterifying nanocellulose with green crosslinkers (Adv. Mater. Interf. 9(16), 2200280, May 2022; ACS Appl. Nano Mater. 5, 5680-5687, April 4, 2022; Carbo. Pol. 320, 121197, November 2023; ACS Omega 9(22) 23442-23450, May 2024; ACS Appl. Energy Mater. 8(1) 267–275, Jan 2025).
2. The synthesis of ECHMCC, UC-CPPR, and CPPR: The authors did not explain clearly how to synthesize them step by step in Methods and Supporting Information. MCC is crystalline cellulose, and ECHMCC seems an amorphous cellulose, as shown in SI Figure 13. It seems that the authors dissolved MCC and performed epoxidation. Once it is true, then the cellulose solvent could influence all of products. The authors need to explain it.
3. The authors should carefully use the acronyms by denoting full names, for example, ECHMCC.
4. The mechanical properties of CPPR (compressive strength of 115.42 MPa and stiffness of 1404.16 MPa) are much lower than the nanocellulose 3D printed results. The authors need to compare their results with previously reported ones.
5. Lines 345-346: “Moreover, the cyclic compression tests confirmed the excellent shape memory 345 recovery function of the material (Fig. 5c).” Fig. 5c shows nothing but pseudo-elastic (or super-elastic) behavior of CPPR material. Once CPPR has shape memory effect, then its quasi-plastic behavior (residual strain) needs to be shown. Otherwise, it may not be appropriate that CPPR has shape memory effect.

### Reviewer 4

The manuscript reports a cellulose-based photo-polymerizable resin for 3D printing that exhibits very promising structural integrity, stress dissipation, and shape-memory behavior. The topic is of interest and the experimental work is substantial. Overall, I believe the manuscript could be suitable for publication in Nature Communications after revision. Blow are my detailed comments.

1. The authors should more clearly place this work in the context of existing 3D-printed shape-memory resins. A dedicated comparison (e.g., table + discussion) to recent reports is required, highlighting the most relevant metrics such as recovery time, recovery ratio, mechanical properties, switching temperature, cycle life, and printing resolution. This will help demonstrate the degree of advancement in a quantitative manner.
2. Recovery time is a key performance index for shape-memory materials. The manuscript should report quantitative recovery data and compare directly with state-of-the-art resins. Please also describe the testing protocol in the Methods section and include appropriate statistics (sample size, mean +/- SD).
3. Some panels are discussed out of sequence (e.g., Figs. 3 and 4: panel 3g/4e discussed before 3f/4b). In addition, Figs. 2–4 (compressive, tensile, shear tests) contain repetitive content and could be consolidated into one or two multi-panel figures for clarity.
4. The statement in lines 69–72 that “our research group has developed …” appears incorrect, as the cited papers seem to be not from the authors’ group. Please review this wording or provide accurate references. A thorough check of the manuscript for similar citation or attribution errors is also necessary.
5. The authors attribute the tensile-strength increase after 100 days in water to “hydrolysis optimizing the structure.” An alternative explanation could be additional hydrogen bonding or physical rearrangement. To clarify the mechanism, the authors may consider: (1) Providing stronger evidence for hydrolysis (e.g., FTIR, XPS, solid-state NMR, molecular weight analysis, and/or TGA); (2) Performing control immersions in hydrogen-bonding vs. non-hydrogen-bonding solvents and reporting the results; and/or (3) Discussing swelling behavior and mass change during immersion.
6. In Fig. 3g and the supporting information, TPO appears to be confused with TPU. Please correct.
7. The manuscript contains some repetition and excessive jargon, which reduces readability. Please streamline the text, remove redundancies, define abbreviations at first use (e.g., CPPR, HMPR, non-ECPR), and simplify language where possible.
8. For all mechanical and shape-memory data, please report sample size (n), statistical measures (mean +/- SD), and test conditions (strain rate, sample dimensions, testing temperature). In addition, provide sufficient details on printing parameters (resin viscosity, printer model/settings, layer thickness, curing conditions) to ensure reproducibility.

The reaction exhibited in Fig. R3 (also see in Fig. S15) of the SI corresponds to Step 3,
which details the photo-initiated free-radical polymerisation of the CPPR resin. First,
150 mL of the CPPR precursor prepared in Step 2 was transferred into a 500 mL round-
bottom flask, followed by the addition of 15 mL of ethylene glycol dimethacrylate
(EGDMA) as a reactive co-monomer for the subsequent free-radical polymerisation.
The mixture was stirred at 50 °C until complete dissolution. Next, the temperature
was lowered to 30 °C (to prevent premature partial polymerisation), and 40 wt%
acrylamide (C₃H₅NO) was introduced as a crosslinker. The reaction was allowed to
proceed under stirring for 30 min at 30 °C. Subsequently, 0.1 wt% N,N′-
methylenebisacrylamide was introduced, and stirring continued for another 30 min.
Finally, 0.5 wt% 2,4,6-trimethylbenzoyl-diphenylphosphine oxide (TPO) was added as
the photoinitiator, and stirring was continued until a homogeneous Cellulose-based
photocurable print resin liquid (CPPR-L) capable of undergoing UV-induced free-
radical polymerization was obtained. The CPPR-L2 and CPPR-L3 were fabricated
according to the different content of CPPR and acrylamide. HEMA-PR refers
photocurable print resin only with HEMA. NE-CPPR refers CPPR without MCC
epichlorohydrin step.

(1)What Fig. R7a shows and what it does not
Under single-cycle tension, HEMA-PR indeed exhibits a slightly higher ultimate tensile
strength (UTS) (27.71 MPa) than CPPR-P (25.16 MPa) in Fig.R7 (also see Fig. 3d, 3b
and 3c in the revised manuscript). Their elastic moduli are essentially comparable
(HEMA-PR: 1412.96 MPa; CPPR-P: 1404.16 MPa). However, HEMA-PR lacks cyclic
recovery and rapidly fails under repeated loading, while CPPR-P maintains a near 100%
stress level across all cycles with clear elastic recovery in Fig. R7b and 7c. These key
distinctions and quantitative values are now explicitly emphasised in the revised text.
Fig. R7 (a) Stress-strain curves obtained under tensile testing ; (b) Stress-strain curves obtained
under cyclic tensile testing; (c) Maximum stress evolution during cyclic tensile testing;.
(2) HEMA-PR (formerly HMPR) composition and behavioural difference
HEMA-PR is a cellulose-free photocurable control formulated using HEMA with the
same photoinitiator family (TPO) and auxiliary crosslinker (EGDMA) used in the
CPPR system. The exact formulation is provided in the Resin Formulations table (Table
R1), with units harmonised across all resin systems. The specific HEMA-PR recipe is:
HEMA 60 wt% (reactive-solids basis), the acrylamide crosslinker ≈40 wt%, TPO 0.5
wt% (of total resin), and the bifunctional additive/crosslinker (EGDMA) was added at
a fixed amount of 15 mL for all experimental groups. Mechanistically, the HEMA-
dominated rigid backbone provides high stiffness but results in intrinsic brittleness,
which severely deteriorates strain-recovery capacity. This is consistent with the
HMPR/HEMA-PR experiments. In contrast, CPPR’s cellulose chains create a
crosslinked network characterised by confined sliding and abundant reversible H-
bonding. This architecture couples high stiffness with recoverability and fatigue
resistance. We have made this contrast explicit in the revised manuscript.
(3) Fair benchmarking and processing details
All test samples were DLP-printed with identical geometry and gage dimensions. The
printing parameters for each resin are listed in Table R2. The default CPPR-L run used
50 μm layers, 8 s per layer, 5 base layers at 13 s, and the specified 405 nm curing/post-
cure. HEMA-PR was printed under its own listed irradiance setpoint to equalise cure
depth/green strength (dose control, E = I×t).
(4) Framing the comparison in the manuscript.
We have clarified that the single-cycle UTS is not the sole or primary figure-of-merit
for this work. The target is the co-optimisation of strength and functional recoverability
under repeated loading. Thus, the manuscript now explicitly states: although HEMA-
PR can reach a marginally higher UTS in one pull, it entirely lacks superelastic/cyclic
recovery or shape-memory capabilities. In contrast, CPPR-P delivers high strength with
robust multi-cycle recovery, which is the central advance demonstrated here (see Figs.
3b–e and the companion cyclic/energy-dissipation data in the Suppplemently Fig. S10).
Take-home message for the reader (in the revised manuscript 199-205 line): HEMA-
PR is marginally stronger at the initial pull but is brittle and non-recoverable. CPPR-P
achieves engineering-level strength and repeatable recovery due to its cellulose-based
network architecture. This is why, despite a modest UTS difference, CPPR-P is the more
suitable material for functional AM components. The paragraph concerning Figs. 3b–e
has been expanded to explicitly separate single-cycle strength from multi-cycle
recoverability/fatigue resistance, citing the exact numbers.

14. In Figure 21 from SI. What is the explanation for such a high weight remaining at
800ºC?
Our response:Thank you for pointing this out. In Fig. R14 (SI Fig. S29), the black
curve corresponds to the uncured liquid CPPR resin (CPPR-L) and the red one to the
DLP-printed, fully cured CPPR specimen (CPPR-P). This is now explicitly stated in
the caption. Thermogravimetry was run under nitrogen up to 800°C (Netzsch STA 449
F3; 20 K min⁻¹), as described in the Methods section. Under this inert atmosphere, both
materials form a carbonaceous char; thus, a non-zero residual mass is expected at 800°
C. The relatively high residual weight at 800°C arises from two primary contributions:
(1) Carbon char formation: Dehydration/aromatisation reactions of the cellulose-
derived segments promote char formation. In addition, the covalently crosslinked
network in the printed CPPR resin further suppresses volatilisation, yielding a higher
char fraction than the uncured blend.
(2) norganic ash residue: The phosphine-oxide photoinitiator (TPO) is known to
generate P-oxide/phosphate residues under pyrolysis. These survive to 800°C and add
to the apparent residual weight.
The high weight remaining at 800°C is not an anomaly, but the sum of: (i) carbon
char favoured by the cellulose-derived and crosslinked chemistries under inert
conditions, and (ii) a small but measurable inorganic residue from the P-containing
photoinitiator. Switching to oxidative TG would remove the char and isolate the true
ash.

After DLP curing, the molecular weight of CPPR-P increases significantly compared to

2. The synthesis of ECHMCC, UC-CPPR, and CPPR: The authors did not explain
clearly how to synthesize them step by step in Methods and Supporting Information.
MCC is crystalline cellulose, and ECHMCC seems an amorphous cellulose, as
shown in SI Figure 13. It seems that the authors dissolved MCC and performed
epoxidation. Once it is true, then the cellulose solvent could influence all of
products. The authors need to explain it.
Our response: Thank you very much for your suggestion. Upon review, we realised
that key methodological details were indeed missing, preventing a clear and
unambiguous description of the synthetic route for obtaining the photocurable resin.
We have now provided sufficient detail to ensure reproducibility of the reaction and
have incorporated this information into the Methods section of the revised manuscript
(lines 439–477). We are grateful to you for pointing out this critical omission.
Synthesis – Step 1 the prepared process of MCC epichlorohydrin.
The reaction shown in Fig. R1(Fig. S13 of the SI) corresponds to Step 1 of the synthesis.
First, an epoxide ring-opening reaction occurs between the cellulose chains and
epichlorohydrin. Briefly, 2 g of pretreated microcrystalline cellulose (MCC) was
initially allowed to swell and uniformly dispersed in 70 mL of DMSO and maintained
at 50°C in a water bath until a homogeneous suspension was obtained. Subsequently,
epichlorohydrin (40 mL) was placed in a dropping funnel and added dropwise at a rate
of 10 mL h⁻¹. Then, 15 mL of 30 wt% aqueous NaOH solution was added dropwise
over 30–45 min using a dropping funnel. The mixture was then heated to 80–85°C and
allowed to react for a further 4 h. After cooling the reaction system to room temperature,
the functionalised MCC precursor was obtained. Under alkaline conditions at 80°C, the
epoxide group of epichlorohydrin underwent a ring-opening reaction to generate
reactive sites, at which point the primary hydroxyl group at the C6 position of cellulose
reacted with it. The resulting product is named as MCC-E.
Fig. R1 Epoxide ring-opening reaction between cellulose molecules and epichlorohydrin.
Synthesis – Step 2 the synthetic of Cellulose-based photopolymerisable resin
(CPPR) precursor .
The reaction depicted in Fig. R2(Fig. 14 of the SI) corresponds to Step 2 of the
synthesis. Based on the precursor obtained in Step 1, free-radical photoreactive groups
were grafted onto the cellulose backbone. The product from Step 1 was transferred into
a 500 mL round-bottom flask and 0.5 wt% methanesulfonic acid (CH₃SO₃H) was used
as a catalyst. Subsequently, 50 wt% hydroxyethyl methacrylate(HEMA) (C₆H₁₀O₃) was
added to introduce the free-radical photoreactive grafting groups, and the mixture was
stirred at 70°C in a water bath for 6 h. After reaction completion, the system was cooled
to 50°C and maintained for a further 4 h to ensure complete conversion. The resulting
product is Cellulose-based photopolymerisable resin (CPPR) precursor used for DLP
additive manufacturing.
Fig. R2 Graft-free radical photosensitive reactive groups.
Synthesis – Step 3 the synthetic of Cellulose-based photocurable print resin liquid
(CPPR-L).
The reaction exhibited in Fig. R3(Fig. 15 of the SI) corresponds to Step 3, which details
the photo-initiated free-radical polymerisation of the CPPR resin. First, 150 mL of the
CPPR resin monomer prepared in Step 2 was transferred into a 500 mL round-bottom
flask, followed by the addition of 15 mL of ethylene glycol dimethacrylate
(EGDMA) as a reactive co-monomer for the subsequent free-radical polymerisation.
The mixture was stirred at 50°C until complete dissolution. Next, the temperature
was lowered to 30°C (to prevent premature partial polymerisation), and 40 wt%
acrylamide (C₃H₅NO) was introduced as a crosslinker. The reaction was allowed to
proceed under stirring for 30 min at 30 °C. Subsequently, 0.1 wt% N,N′-
methylenebisacrylamide (MBA) was introduced, and stirring continued for another 30 min.
Finally, 0.5 wt% TPO was added as the photoinitiator, and stirring was continued until a
homogeneous Cellulose-based photocurable print resin liquid (CPPR-L) capable of
undergoing UV-induced free-radical polymerization was obtained. The CPPR-L2 and
CPPR-L3 were fabricated according to the different content of CPPR and acrylamide.
HEMA-PR refers photocurable print resin only with HEMA. NE-CPPR refers CPPR
without MCC epichlorohydrin step.
Fig.R3 DLP-based UV curing via free radical polymerisation and crosslinking.
Regarding the issue you raised in your revision comments concerning MCC dissolution
and the change in crystallinity (SI Fig. S23), we would like to thank you for pointing
this out, as it helps make our manuscript more scientifically rigorous and easier to
follow.
First, we did not dissolve MCC in a cellulose-dissolving medium (such as DMAc/LiCl,
ionic liquids, or NaOH/urea). Step 1 is explicitly conducted in a heterogeneous
alkaline system at 80 °C, where MCC is in a swollen/dispersed state. ECH reacts with
the C6–OH groups of MCC via epoxide ring-opening etherification and results in a
small degree of interchain bridging; it is not a dissolution process mediated by “true
cellulose solvents”.
The supporting data and analytical evidence confirm this:
(1) The process description in SI Fig. S13 clearly states “alkaline conditions at 80°
C, with C6 participating in the reaction”, which indicates that ECH reacts mainly
with primary hydroxyls at the C6 position to form ether linkages and occasional
interchain bridges.
(2) Fig. R4 (SI Fig. S22) FTIR shows the appearance/intensification of C–O–C bands
at 1120–1160 cm⁻¹.
Fig. R4 FTIR spectra of microcrystalline cellulose (MCC) raw materials and epichlorohydrin-
modified cellulose molecules (MCC-E) via ring-opening epoxidation (Synthesis - Step 1).
(3) Fig. R5 (SI Fig. S20) ¹H NMR reveals a new signal region at 3.6–4.2 ppm.
Fig. R5 1H NMR spectra of MCC molecular raw material and epichlorohydrin-modified
cellulose molecules via ring-opening epoxidation (Synthesis - Step 1).
(4) Fig. R6 (SI Fig. S23) XRD demonstrates only a decrease in the
intensity/crystallinity of the cellulose I (002) reflection, without conversion to
cellulose II or the presence of a fully amorphous halo.
Fig. R6 XRD patterns of MCC raw materials and epichlorohydrin-modified cellulose
derivatives via ring-opening epoxidation (Synthesis - Step 1).
Taken together, these features are indicative of substitution-induced disorder, rather
than a dissolution–regeneration pathway of cellulose. The XRD changes are consistent
with the chemical “anchors” observed via FTIR/NMR and can be attributed to
etherification substitution + local crosslinking that disrupts the hydrogen-bond network,
rather than to any solvent-induced regeneration process.
Furthermore, after Step 2 (HEMA grafting), the crystalline form and overall
crystallinity of the material remain essentially unchanged (SI Fig. S25). This further
supports that the “apparent amorphisation” originates from chemical substitution and
hydrogen-bond disruption, and that no dissolution–regeneration of cellulose has
occurred.
In Step 3, the acrylamide network introduced by photocuring may induce new ordered
peaks in the XRD patterns of the DLP-printed samples (SI Fig. S12). This reflects an
increase in order associated with the final covalent network, which is not contradictory
to the “local disordering” observed in the first two steps. Instead, it represents a new
order parameter that emerges only following DLP printing and curing.
As regards the concern that “the solvent may affect all products”, we explicitly state in
the Methods section that no cellulose-dissolving solvent system was utilised in the
synthetic procedures. DMSO-d₆ was employed only as a characterisation solvent for
NMR measurements (on separately prepared samples) and was not involved in any
other synthetic pathways.

5. Lines 345-346: “Moreover, the cyclic compression tests confirmed the excellent
shape memory 345 recovery function of the material (Fig. 5c).” Fig. 5c shows
nothing but pseudo-elastic (or super-elastic) behavior of CPPR material. Once
CPPR has shape memory effect, then its quasi-plastic behavior (residual strain)
needs to be shown. Otherwise, it may not be appropriate that CPPR has shape
memory effect.
Our response: We appreciate the reviewer’s observation and agree that the original
Fig. 5c demonstrated a thermal pseudo-elastic (superelastic-like) recovery under cyclic
compression at room temperature, which alone is insufficient to evidence thermally
triggered shape-memory effect (SME). To definitely address this concern, we have
performed additional thermally triggered shape memory experiments, and the results
are presented in the Supplementary Materials. In these new tests, the material was
programmed into a temporary shape via tensile loading and then heated to 100°C to
trigger shape recovery (Table.R3). The shape memory performance is now
quantitatively confirmed by a high shape fixity ratio (Rf), a high shape recovery ratio
(Rr), and a rapid recovery time (Tr). All these metrics demonstrate that the deformed
shape is fully fixed at room temperature and almost completely recovered upon heating.
We have also included a video in the SI showing the sample programming, shape
fixation at room temperature, and subsequent recovery upon heating, providing clear
